fields.description: John Bunyan's account of his own conversion — the years of terror, doubt and half-heard verses that ran before The Pilgrim's Progress. Unsparing about despair, and one of the first books in English to describe an ordinary man's inner life from the inside.

fields.title: Publisher’s Foreward
fields.body_html:
PUBLISHER’S FOREWORD

John Bunyan was born at Elstow, near Bedford, England, sometime in the fall of 1628, the first of three children born to Thomas and Margaret Bunyan. The parish register indicates that he was baptized on November 30, 1628.

In Grace Abounding Bunyan describes his descent as “of a low and inconsiderable generation.” He had particular disdain for his father’s house; to him it was “of a rank that is meanest and most despised of all the families in the land.”

Sir Walter Scott thought John Bunyan was of gypsy descent, because his father was a traveling tinker, a mender of pots and pans. But historians view the occupation as somewhat like that of “village blacksmith.” The Bunyans were not homeless; they were landowners, but of peasant stock.

Bunyan’s schooling was of brief duration, and it wasn’t long before he was assisting his father and learning the trade himself. On his sixteenth birthday Bunyan joined Cromwell’s New Model Army, introducing him to the Puritan movement. After this military stint, he settled down as a tinker (“brazier”) and married at the age of twenty.

In 1653 Bunyan joined the Puritan Free Church in Bedford, and in 1657 he took on his first assignment as a “field preacher.” At this time there were scores of men, most with little education, who were preaching to Nonconformist audiences throughout England. With the restoration of Charles II to the throne, these preachers were suspect and subject to arrest. Refusing to refrain from preaching, Bunyan was arrested in 1660 and imprisoned for more than eleven years.

Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, written during this imprisonment, is the spiritual autobiography of Bunyan, the traveling tinker who became the eminent preacher and author. It is in the genre of Augustine’s Confessions and Thomas a Kempis’s Imitation of Christ. It is not a detailed account of Bunyan’s early life, for it tells us very little of his youth, education, military experiences, and marriages.

Written in 1666, Grace Abounding chronicles Bunyan’s spiritual journey from a profane life filled with cursing, blasphemy, and Sabbath desecration to a new creation in Christ Jesus. Some commentators on Bunyan’s life and work are of the opinion that Bunyan wrote too disparagingly of his early life. George Offor, editor of a three volume compilation of Bunyan’s works, observes:

A great difference of opinion has been expressed by learned men as to whether Bunyan’s account of himself is to be understood literally, as it respects his bad conduct before his conversion, or whether he views himself through a glass, by which his evil habits are magnified. No one can doubt his perfect honesty. He plainly narrates his bad, as well as his redeeming qualities; nor does his narrative appear to be exaggerated.

Grace Abounding is an autobiography that begins with guilt and despair and ends with a heart “full of comfort,” a thankful heart for “grace abounding.”

Those who have read both Grace Abounding and The Pilgrim’s Progress will realize that The Pilgrim’s Progress, in substantial measure, is the same life as that described in Grace Abounding, but in allegory rather than straightforward narrative. George Offor makes this point when he quotes a Dr. Cheever:

As you read the “Grace Abounding”, you are ready to say at every step, Here is the future author of the “Pilgrim’s Progress”. It is as if you stood beside some great sculptor, and watched every movement of the chisel, having seen his design; so that at every blow some new trait of beauty in the future comes clearly into view.

Ernest W. Bacon, in a recent biography based on the latest historical research makes the same point:

The experiences he [Bunyan] records in Grace Abounding are seen in the characters of The Pilgrim’s Progress, and there is little doubt that he could not have written the great allegory had he not experienced God’s saving mercy recounted in the autobiography. It has an undying vitality and perpetual youth about it, is a record of Puritan experience unsurpassed, and a spiritual stimulus of great value.

The importance of Grace Abounding is summed up by Hugh Martin:

Grace Abounding is among the greatest stories of God’s dealings with the human soul—to be put on the shelf beside such treasures as Augustine’s Confessions, Law’s Serious Call, Baxter’s Autobiography, and Wesley’s account of his own spiritual travail.

fields.title: A Preface, or Brief Account of the Publishing of This Work
fields.body_html:
A PREFACE

OR BRIEF ACCOUNT OF THE PUBLISHING OF THIS WORK

WRITTEN BY THE AUTHOR THEREOF, AND DEDICATED TO THOSE WHOM GOD HATH COUNTED HIM WORTHY TO BEGET TO FAITH, BY HIS MINISTRY IN THE WORD

CHILDREN, grace be with you. Amen. I have been taken away from you in person, and am so tied up that I cannot carry out the duty God lays on me toward you, for your further building up in faith and holiness. Yet so that you may see that my soul has a fatherly care for, and longing after, your spiritual and everlasting welfare, I now once again look out after you all, as I did before from the top of Shenir and Hermon, so now from the lions’ dens, from the mountains of the leopards (Song 4:8), greatly longing to see you arrive safely in the desired haven.

I thank God every time I remember you. And I rejoice, even while I am stuck between the teeth of the lions in the wilderness, at the grace and mercy and knowledge of Christ our Saviour that God has given you, with an abundance of faith and love. Your hunger and thirst for a deeper acquaintance with the Father in His Son, your tenderness of heart, your trembling at sin, and your sober and holy conduct before both God and people are a great refreshment to me. ‘For ye are our glory and joy’ (1 Thess. 2:20).

I have sent you, enclosed here, a drop of the honey I have taken out of the carcass of a lion (Judg. 14:5–9). I have eaten some of it myself, and am greatly refreshed by it. (Temptations, when we first meet them, are like the lion that roared at Samson; but if we overcome them, the next time we see them we shall find a nest of honey inside them.) The Philistines do not understand me. It is an account of the work of God on my own soul, from the very first until now, in which you may see my castings down and my liftings up; for He wounds, and His hands make whole. It is written in the Scripture, ‘The father to the children shall make known thy truth’ (Isa. 38:19). Yes, this is why I lay so long at Sinai (Deut. 4:10–11), to see the fire, the cloud and the darkness: so that I might fear the Lord all the days of my life on earth, and tell my children of His wonderful works (Ps. 78:3–5).

Moses wrote of the journeys of the children of Israel from Egypt to the land of Canaan (Num. 33:1–2), and also commanded them to remember their forty years of travel in the wilderness. ‘Thou shalt remember all the way which the Lord thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart, whether thou wouldest keep his commandments, or no’ (Deut. 8:2). So I have tried to do this; and not only that, but to publish it as well, so that, if God wills, others may be reminded of what He has done for their souls by reading of His work on me.

It is good for Christians to call to mind often the very beginnings of grace in their souls. ‘It is a night to be much observed unto the Lord for bringing them out from the land of Egypt: this is that night of the Lord to be observed of all the children of Israel in their generations’ (Exod. 12:42). ‘O my God,’ says David, ‘my soul is cast down within me: therefore will I remember thee from the land of Jordan, and of the Hermonites, from the hill Mizar’ (Ps. 42:6). He also remembered the lion and the bear when he went to fight the giant of Gath (1 Sam. 17:36–37).

It was Paul’s habit (Acts 22), even when he was on trial for his life (Acts 24), always to set out before his judges the way he was converted. He would think of that day and that hour in which he first met with grace, for he found it a support to him. When God had brought the children of Israel through the Red Sea and far into the wilderness, they still had to turn right round and go back there, to remember the drowning of their enemies (Num. 14:25). For though they had sung His praise before, ‘they soon forgat his works’ (Ps. 106:11–13).

In this account of mine you may see much; much, I say, of the grace of God toward me. I thank God I can count it much, for it was greater than my sins, and greater than Satan’s temptations too. I can remember my fears and doubts and sad months with comfort; they are like the head of Goliath in my hand. There was nothing for David like Goliath’s sword, the very sword that should have been sheathed in his own belly; for the very sight and memory of it preached God’s deliverance to him. Oh, the memory of my great sins, of my great temptations, and of my great fears of perishing for ever! They bring back to my mind afresh the memory of my great help, my great support from heaven, and the great grace God showed to such a wretch as I.

My dear children, call to mind the former days, the years of long ago. Remember also your songs in the night, and commune with your own heart (Ps. 77:5–12). Yes, look carefully, and leave no corner of it unsearched, for there is treasure hidden there: the treasure of your first and second experience of the grace of God toward you. Remember, I say, the word that first took hold of you. Remember your terrors of conscience, and your fear of death and hell. Remember also your tears and prayers to God, and how you sighed for mercy under every hedge. Have you no hill Mizar to remember? Have you forgotten the field, the milk house, the stable, the barn and the like, where God visited your soul? Remember also the word, the word, I say, on which the Lord has caused you to hope. If you have sinned against light; if you are tempted to blaspheme; if you are down in despair; if you think God is fighting against you; or if heaven is hidden from your eyes; remember that it was like this with your father, but the Lord delivered me out of it all.

I could have said much more in this account about my temptations and troubles over sin, and also about the merciful kindness and working of God with my soul. I could also have taken up a much loftier style than the one I have used here, and could have decorated everything more than I seem to have done, but I dare not. God was not playing when He convicted me; the devil was not playing when he tempted me; nor was I playing when I sank as into a bottomless pit, when the pangs of hell took hold of me. So I may not play in telling of them, but must be plain and simple, and set the thing down as it was. Whoever likes it, let him receive it; and whoever does not, let him produce a better. Farewell.

My dear children, the milk and honey lie beyond this wilderness. God be merciful to you, and grant that you are not lazy about going in to possess the land.

fields.title: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners; Or, a Brief Relation of the Exceeding Mercy of God in Christ, to His Poor Servant John Bunyan
fields.body_html:
GRACE ABOUNDING TO THE CHIEF OF SINNERS;

OR, A BRIEF RELATION OF THE EXCEEDING MERCY OF GOD IN CHRIST, TO HIS POOR SERVANT JOHN BUNYAN

1. In this account of God’s merciful working on my soul, it will not be out of place first to give you, in a few words, a hint of my family and upbringing, so that the goodness and generosity of God toward me may be all the more exalted and magnified before the children of men.

2. As for my descent, then, it was, as many know well, of a low and insignificant family, my father’s house being of the rank that is lowest and most despised of all the families in the land. So I have nothing here, as others have, to boast of in the way of noble blood or high birth according to the flesh. Yet, all things considered, I praise the heavenly Majesty that it was by this door He brought me into the world, to share in the grace and life that is in Christ by the gospel.

3. But in spite of the lowliness and insignificance of my parents, it pleased God to put it into their hearts to send me to school, to learn to read and write. This I did learn, to the same level as other poor men’s children; though, to my shame I confess, I soon lost the little I learned, almost completely, and long before the Lord worked His gracious work of conversion on my soul.

4. As for my own natural life, during the time I was without God in the world, it was indeed ‘according to the course of this world,’ and according to ‘the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience’ (Eph. 2:2–3). It was my delight to be ‘taken captive by him at his will’ (2 Tim. 2:26). I was filled with all unrighteousness, which worked so strongly and showed itself so much in both my heart and my life, and that from childhood, that I had few equals, especially considering my years, which were tender and few, in cursing, swearing, lying and blaspheming the holy name of God.

5. Indeed, I was so settled and rooted in these things that they became second nature to me. And as I have soberly considered since, this so offended the Lord that even in my childhood He scared and frightened me with fearful dreams and terrified me with dreadful visions. Often, after I had spent one day and another in sin, I have been greatly troubled in my bed, while asleep, by imaginings of devils and wicked spirits, who, as I thought then, were always trying to drag me away with them, and I could never be rid of them.

6. At that age, too, I would be greatly troubled and distressed by thoughts of the day of judgment, both night and day, and would tremble at the thought of the fearful torments of hellfire, always afraid that it would be my lot to be found at last among those devils and hellish fiends who are bound there with the chains and bonds of eternal darkness, ‘unto the judgment of the great day.’

7. These things, I say, so distressed my soul when I was only a child of nine or ten that I was often very downcast and troubled in my mind by them, even in the middle of my many games and childish vanities, among my empty companions. Yet I could not let go of my sins. Indeed, I was also so overcome then with despair of life and heaven that I would often wish either that there were no hell, or that I were a devil, supposing they were only tormentors; so that, if I really had to go there, I might be a tormentor rather than be tormented myself.

8. A while later these terrible dreams left me, and I soon forgot them too, for my pleasures quickly cut off the memory of them, as if they had never been. So, more greedily, as far as the strength of my nature allowed, I still gave free rein to my lusts and delighted in every transgression against the law of God. So until I married, I was the very ringleader of all the young people who kept me company, in every kind of vice and ungodliness.

9. Indeed, the lusts and fruits of the flesh had such a hold on this poor soul of mine that, if a miracle of precious grace had not prevented it, I would not only have perished by the stroke of eternal justice, but would also have laid myself open to the stroke of those laws that bring some people to disgrace and open shame before the world.

10. In those days the thought of religion was very grievous to me. I could not stand it myself, nor stand anyone else having it, so that when I saw some reading books about Christian devotion, it was like a prison to me. Then I said to God, ‘Depart from us; for we desire not the knowledge of thy ways’ (Job 21:14). I was now empty of all good thoughts. Heaven and hell were both out of sight and mind, and as for being saved or damned, they were the last things I thought of. O Lord, You know my life, and my ways were not hidden from You.

11. Yet I remember this well: though I could sin myself with the greatest delight and ease, and also took pleasure in the vileness of my companions, even then, if I ever saw wicked things done by those who professed goodness, it would make my spirit tremble. Once above all, when I was at the height of my vanity, I heard someone who was regarded as a religious man swear, and it struck my spirit so hard that it made my heart ache.

12. But God did not leave me altogether. He still followed me, not now with convictions but with judgments, though judgments mixed with mercy. Once I fell into a creek of the sea and barely escaped drowning. Another time I fell out of a boat into the river at Bedford, but mercy still kept me alive. Besides, another time, when I was in the fields with one of my companions, an adder happened to cross the road. I had a stick in my hand, so I struck it across the back, and having stunned it, I forced its mouth open with my stick and pulled its sting out with my fingers. If God had not been merciful, I might have brought myself to my end by this reckless act.

13. I have also noticed this with thanksgiving. When I was a soldier, I was one of those picked to go to a certain place to besiege it. But just as I was ready to go, one of the company asked to go in my place. When I agreed, he took my place, and when he came to the siege, as he stood on sentry duty, he was shot in the head with a musket ball and died.

14. Here, as I said, were judgments and mercy, but neither of them awakened my soul to righteousness. So I went on sinning, and grew more and more rebellious against God and careless about my own salvation.

15. Soon after this I married, and my mercy was to find a wife whose father was regarded as godly. This woman and I came together as poor as poor could be, without so much as a dish or a spoon between us. Yet she had this as her share: The Plain Man’s Pathway to Heaven and The Practice of Piety, which her father had left her when he died. I would sometimes read these two books with her, and found some things in them that pleased me somewhat; but all this while I met with no conviction. She would also often tell me what a godly man her father was, and how he would rebuke and correct vice, both in his house and among his neighbours, and what a strict and holy life he lived in his day, in both word and deed.

16. So these books, with what she told me, though they did not reach my heart to awaken it to my sad and sinful state, did stir up in me some desire for religion. So, because I knew no better, I threw myself very eagerly into the religion of the times: going to church twice a day, and among the foremost too, and there very devoutly saying and singing as others did, while keeping up my wicked life. But along with this I was so overrun with a spirit of superstition that I adored, and with great devotion, absolutely everything: the high place, the priest, the clerk, the vestments, the service and whatever else belonged to the church. I counted everything in it holy, and especially thought the priest and clerk most happy and without doubt greatly blessed, because they were, as I thought then, the servants of God, and chief in the holy temple to do His work there.

17. In a short time this notion grew so strong in my spirit that, had I only seen a priest, however filthy and debauched his life, I would find my spirit bowing down under him, revering him and bound to him. Indeed, I thought that, because of the love I had for them, supposing them to be ministers of God, I could have lain down at their feet and let them trample on me. Their name, their dress and their work so intoxicated and bewitched me.

18. After I had been like this for a considerable time, another thought came into my mind: whether we were Israelites or not. For finding in the Scriptures that they were once God’s special people, I thought that if I were one of this race, my soul must surely be happy. Now again I found in myself a great longing to have this question settled, but could not tell how to do it. At last I asked my father about it, and he told me no, we were not. So my spirits sank as far as that hope was concerned, and stayed that way.

19. But all this while I was not aware of the danger and evil of sin. I was kept from considering that sin would damn me, whatever religion I followed, unless I was found in Christ. Indeed, I never thought of Him, or of whether there was such a one or not. So a man wanders while he is blind, but only wearies himself with vanity, for he does not know the way to the city of God (Eccles. 10:15).

20. But one day, among all the sermons our parson preached, his subject was the Sabbath day, and the evil of breaking it, whether with work, sports or otherwise. Now I, in spite of my religion, was someone who took great delight in every kind of vice, and that was especially the day I amused myself with it. So my conscience fell under his sermon, and I thought and believed that he had preached that sermon on purpose to show me my wrongdoing. At that time I felt what guilt was, though never before, as far as I can remember. But then, for the moment, I was greatly weighed down with it, and so I went home when the sermon was over with a great burden on my spirit.

21. For the moment this numbed the sinews of my best pleasures and made my former delights bitter to me. But see, it did not last. Before I had properly finished dinner, the trouble began to go off my mind, and my heart went back to its old course. Oh, how glad I was that this trouble had gone from me, and that the fire was put out, so that I could sin again without restraint! So when I had satisfied nature with my food, I shook the sermon out of my mind and went back with great delight to my old habit of sports and games.

22. But that same day, as I was in the middle of a game of tip-cat, and had struck the cat one blow from the hole, just as I was about to strike it a second time, a voice suddenly darted from heaven into my soul, which said, “Wilt thou leave thy sins and go to heaven, or have thy sins and go to hell?” At this I was thrown into utter amazement. So, leaving my cat on the ground, I looked up to heaven, and it was as if I had seen, with the eyes of my understanding, the Lord Jesus looking down on me, very hotly displeased with me, and as if He were severely threatening me with some grievous punishment for these and other ungodly practices.

23. No sooner had I formed this in my mind than suddenly this conclusion was fastened on my spirit, for the first hint had set my sins before my face again: that I had been a great and grievous sinner, and that it was now too late for me to seek heaven, for Christ would not forgive me or pardon my transgressions. Then I fell to musing on this too, and while I was thinking about it and fearing it might be so, I felt my heart sink in despair, concluding that it was too late. So I resolved in my mind that I would go on in sin. For, I thought, if this is how things are, my state is surely miserable: miserable if I leave my sins, and only miserable if I follow them. I can only be damned, and if I must be, I might as well be damned for many sins as for few.

24. So I stood there in the middle of my game, in front of everyone who was there, though I told them nothing. But, I say, having reached this conclusion, I went back desperately to my sport. And I remember well that at once this kind of despair so possessed my soul that I was persuaded I could never have any other comfort than what I could get in sin. Heaven was already gone, so I must not think about that. So I found in myself a great desire to take my fill of sin, always studying what sin there was to commit, so that I might taste its sweetness. And I made as much haste as I could to fill my belly with its delicacies, in case I died before I had my desire, for I was very afraid of that. In these things, I swear before God, I am not lying, nor am I putting on this way of speaking. These really were my desires, strongly and with all my heart. May the good Lord, whose mercy is beyond searching out, forgive me my transgressions.

25. And I am very confident that this temptation of the devil is more common among poor creatures than many realize. He overruns their spirits with a sour and seared state of heart and a numbing of conscience, and quietly and slyly supplies that state with such despair that, though the soul does not feel much guilt, they constantly have a secret conclusion within them that there is no hope for them; for they have loved sins, ‘and after them will I go’ (Jer. 2:25; 18:12).

26. So now I went on in sin with great greed of mind, always resenting that I could not be as satisfied with it as I wanted. This went on with me for about a month or more. But one day, as I was standing at a neighbour’s shop window, cursing and swearing and playing the madman in my usual way, the woman of the house was sitting inside and heard me. Though she was a very loose and ungodly wretch herself, she declared that I swore and cursed so fearfully that she trembled to hear me. She told me further that I was the most ungodly fellow for swearing she had ever heard in all her life, and that by doing this I was capable of spoiling all the young people in a whole town if they only came into my company.

27. At this rebuke I was silenced and put to secret shame, and that too, as I thought, before the God of heaven. So while I stood there, hanging my head, I wished with all my heart that I could be a little child again, so that my father could teach me to speak without this wicked habit of swearing. For, I thought, I am so used to it that it is useless for me to think of reforming; I thought it could never happen.

28. But how it came about I do not know: from that time on I gave up my swearing so completely that it was a great wonder to me to see it. Whereas before I did not know how to speak without putting an oath before and another after, to give my words authority, now I could speak better without it, and more pleasantly, than I ever could before. All this while I did not know Jesus Christ, nor did I give up my sports and games.

29. But soon after this I fell in with a poor man who professed religion, who, as I thought then, talked pleasantly about the Scriptures and matters of religion. So, coming to love and like what he said, I took up my Bible and began to take great pleasure in reading it, but especially the historical parts. As for Paul’s letters and Scriptures of that kind, I could not bear them, being still ignorant both of the corruption of my nature and of my need of Jesus Christ to save me, and His worth.

30. So I took up some outward reformation, both in my words and in my life, and set the commandments before me as my way to heaven. I also tried to keep these commandments, and, as I thought, sometimes kept them pretty well, and then I would have comfort. Yet every now and then I would break one, and so trouble my conscience. But then I would repent and say I was sorry for it, and promise God to do better next time, and so get help again; for then I thought I pleased God as well as any man in England.

31. I carried on like this for about a year. All that time our neighbours took me to be a very godly man, a new and religious man, and were amazed to see such a great and striking change in my life and behaviour. And it really was so, though I still did not know Christ, or grace, or faith, or hope. As I have seen clearly since, if I had died then, my state would have been most fearful. This, I say, went on for about a year or more.

32. My neighbours were astonished at my great conversion from outrageous profanity to something like a moral life, and they had good reason to be, for my conversion was as great as if a madman from Bedlam had become a sober man. So they began to praise me, to commend me and to speak well of me, both to my face and behind my back. Now, they said, I had become godly; now I had become a truly honest man. And oh, when I heard that this was what they said and thought of me, it pleased me very much. For though I was still nothing but a poor painted hypocrite, I loved to be talked of as someone truly godly. I was proud of my godliness, and everything I did was done either to be seen by people or to be well spoken of by them. And I carried on like this for about a year or more.

33. You must know that before this I had taken great delight in bell-ringing. But as my conscience began to grow tender, I thought the practice was empty, and so I forced myself to give it up. Yet my mind still hankered after it, so I would go to the church tower and watch, though I dared not ring. But I thought this did not suit religion either. Still I forced myself and went on watching. But soon afterwards I began to think, What if one of the bells should fall? So I chose to stand under a main beam that ran across the tower from side to side, thinking I would be safe there. But then I would think again: if the bell fell while swinging, it might hit the wall first, bounce back onto me and kill me in spite of the beam. This made me stand in the tower doorway. Now, I thought, I am safe enough, for if a bell should fall, I can slip out behind these thick walls and be saved all the same.

34. After this I would still go to watch them ring, but I would go no further than the tower door. Then it came into my head, What if the tower itself should fall? And this thought, that for all I knew it might fall while I stood there watching, shook my mind so constantly that I dared not stand at the tower door any longer, but was forced to run away for fear the tower would fall on my head.

35. Another thing was my dancing. It was a full year before I could give that up entirely. But all this while, whenever I thought I was keeping this or that commandment, or doing anything in word or deed that I thought was good, I had great peace in my conscience. I would think to myself, God cannot help being pleased with me now. Indeed, to put it in my own way, I thought no man in England could please God better than I did.

36. But, poor wretch that I was, all this time I knew nothing of Jesus Christ, and was trying to establish my own righteousness. I would have perished in it if God in His mercy had not shown me more of my natural state.

37. But one day the good providence of God brought me to Bedford to work at my trade. In one of the streets of that town I came upon three or four poor women sitting in a doorway in the sun, talking about the things of God. Wanting now to hear them talk, I drew near to listen to what they said, for by now I was a ready talker myself on religious subjects. But I can say that I heard and did not understand, for they were far above me, out of my reach. They were talking about a new birth, the work of God in their hearts, and how they had been convinced of their miserable state by nature. They talked about how God had visited their souls with His love in the Lord Jesus, and with what words and promises they had been refreshed, comforted and supported against the temptations of the devil. Besides this, they discussed the particular suggestions and temptations of Satan, and told each other which ones had troubled them and how they had been held up under his attacks. They also talked about the wretchedness of their own hearts and their unbelief, and they despised, belittled and loathed their own righteousness as filthy and unable to do them any good.

38. It seemed to me that they spoke as if joy made them speak. They spoke with such delight in the language of Scripture, and with such signs of grace in everything they said, that they seemed to me like people who had found a new world, as if they were a people who dwelt alone and were not to be counted among their neighbours (Num. 23:9).

39. At this I felt my own heart begin to shake, for I suspected my condition was worthless. I saw that in all my thoughts about religion and salvation, the new birth had never entered my mind. I did not know the comfort of the Word and promise, nor the deceitfulness and treachery of my own wicked heart. As for secret thoughts, I took no notice of them. Nor did I understand what Satan’s temptations were, or how they were to be withstood and resisted, and so on.

40. So when I had heard and thought over what they said, I left them and went back to my work. But their talk went with me, and my heart lingered with them, for I was deeply moved by their words. By them I was convinced that I lacked the true marks of a truly godly man, and I was also convinced of the happy and blessed condition of anyone who had them.

41. So I often made it my business to go again and again into the company of these poor people, for I could not stay away. The more I went among them, the more I questioned my condition. As I still remember, I soon found two things in me that sometimes amazed me, especially considering what a blind, ignorant, base and ungodly wretch I had been just before. The first was a great softness and tenderness of heart, which brought me under conviction of what they declared from Scripture. The second was a strong inclination of my mind to meditate continually on it, and on all the other good things I heard or read about at any time.

42. Through these things my mind was now so changed that it clung like a horse leech to the vein, still crying out, Give, give (Prov. 30:15). Indeed, it was so fixed on eternity and on the things of the kingdom of heaven, so far as I knew them, though God knows I knew very little as yet, that neither pleasures nor profits, persuasions nor threats, could loosen it or make it let go its hold. And though I say it with shame, it is truly a fact that it would then have been as hard for me to turn my mind from heaven to earth as I have often found it since to turn it back again from earth to heaven.

43. There is one thing I must not leave out. There was a young man in our town to whom my heart was more closely bound than to anyone else. But he was a most wicked creature for cursing and swearing and sleeping around, so I now shook him off and stopped keeping his company. About three months after I had left him, I met him in a lane and asked him how he was. He answered, in his old swearing and wild way, that he was well. “But, Harry,” I said, “why do you swear and curse like this? What will become of you if you die in this condition?” He answered me in a great temper, “What would the devil do for company, if it were not for such as I am?”

44. About this time I came across some books by the Ranters, put out by some of our countrymen, which were also highly thought of by several long-standing professors of religion. I read some of them but could not form a judgment about them. So as I read them and thought about them, feeling unable to judge, I turned to heartfelt prayer in this way: O Lord, I am a fool, and not able to tell truth from error. Lord, do not leave me to my own blindness, either to approve or condemn this teaching. If it is from God, let me not despise it; if it is from the devil, let me not embrace it. Lord, I lay my soul in this matter only at Your feet; let me not be deceived, I humbly beg You. All this while I had one close religious companion, the poor man I spoke of before. But about this time he too became a thoroughly devilish Ranter and gave himself up to every kind of filthiness, especially sexual immorality. He would also deny that there was a God, an angel or a spirit, and would laugh at every appeal to live soberly. When I tried hard to rebuke his wickedness, he laughed all the more, and claimed that he had gone through every religion and had never hit on the right one until now. He also told me that before long we would see all professing Christians turn to the ways of the Ranters. So, loathing those cursed principles, I left his company at once and became as great a stranger to him as I had once been a close friend.

45. Nor was this man my only temptation. Since my trade took me around the country, I happened to fall into the company of several people who, though strict in religion before, had also been swept away by these Ranters. They too would talk to me about their ways and condemn me as legalistic and in the dark, claiming that they alone had reached perfection, since they could do whatever they liked and not sin. Oh, these temptations suited my flesh, for I was only a young man and my nature was in its prime. But God, who had, I hope, intended me for better things, kept me in the fear of His name and did not let me accept such principles. And blessed be God, who put it into my heart to cry to Him to be kept and guided, still distrusting my own wisdom. For I have since seen the result of that prayer, in His keeping me not only from the errors of the Ranters but also from those that have sprung up since. The Bible was precious to me in those days.

46. And now, it seemed to me, I began to look into the Bible with new eyes, and to read as I never had before. The letters of the apostle Paul were especially sweet and pleasant to me. In fact, I was never out of the Bible then, either reading or meditating on it, and I was always crying out to God that I might know the truth and the way to heaven and glory.

47. As I went on reading, I came upon this passage: ‘To one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge by the same Spirit; and to another faith,’ etc. (1 Cor. 12:8-9). I have since seen that in this Scripture the Holy Spirit chiefly means extraordinary things. Yet at that time it fastened on me with the conviction that I lacked ordinary things, even the understanding and wisdom that other Christians had. I brooded on this word and did not know what to do. This word faith especially troubled me, for I could not help sometimes questioning whether I had any faith or not. I feared that this shut me out of all the blessings that God had given other good people. Yet I was unwilling to conclude that I had no faith in my soul, for if I do that, I thought, I will count myself a castaway indeed.

48. Now, I said to myself, though I am convinced that I am an ignorant fool, and that I lack those blessed gifts of knowledge and understanding that other good people have, yet at a guess I will conclude that I am not altogether without faith, though I do not know what faith is. For it was shown to me, and that, as I have since seen, by Satan, that those who conclude they are without faith have neither rest nor peace in their souls. And I was unwilling to fall into complete despair.

49. So by this suggestion I was for a while made afraid to see my lack of faith. But God would not let me undo and destroy my soul in this way. Against this blind and sad conclusion of mine, He kept raising in me such questions, such fears that I might be deceiving myself in this, that I could not rest content until I came to some certain knowledge of whether I had faith or not. This was always running through my mind: But what if you really lack faith? But how can you tell if you have faith? And besides, I saw for certain that if I did not have it, I was sure to perish for ever.

50. So although at first I tried to overlook the matter of faith, before long, thinking it over better, I was willing to put myself to the test of whether I had faith or not. But alas, poor wretch, I was so ignorant and dull that I had no more idea how to do it than I would know how to begin and complete some rare and intricate piece of craftsmanship that I had never seen or thought about.

51. While I was thinking about this and was at my wits’ end over it (for you must know that I had not yet opened my mind about it to anyone, but only listened and thought), the tempter came in with his delusion: that the only way for me to know I had faith was by trying to work a miracle. He pressed on me those Scriptures that seem to point that way, to drive home and strengthen his temptation. Indeed, one day as I was between Elstow and Bedford, the temptation came hot upon me to test whether I had faith by working a miracle. The miracle at that time was this: I must say to the puddles in the horse tracks, Be dry, and to the dry places, Be puddles. And truly, at one point I was about to say it. But just as I was about to speak, this thought came into my mind: But go under that hedge over there and pray first, that God would make you able. But when I had decided to pray, this came hot upon me: that if I prayed, and came back and tried to do it, and still nothing happened, then I could be sure I had no faith but was a castaway and lost. No, I thought, if that is how it is, I will not try yet, but will wait a little longer.

52. So I remained at a great loss. For I thought that if only those had faith who could do such wonderful things, then I had to conclude that for the present I did not have it, and that I was never likely to have it in the future either. So I was tossed between the devil and my own ignorance, and was so perplexed, especially at certain times, that I did not know what to do.

53. About this time, the state and happiness of these poor people at Bedford was shown to me like this, in a dream or vision. I saw them as if they were sitting on the sunny side of a high mountain, refreshing themselves in the pleasant rays of the sun, while I was shivering and shrinking in the cold, troubled by frost, snow and dark clouds. It seemed to me too that between me and them I saw a wall that ran right round this mountain. My soul longed to pass through this wall, and I decided that if I could, I would go into the very middle of them and comfort myself there with the heat of their sun as well.

54. I thought I went round this wall again and again, searching as I went to see if I could find some way or passage by which I might get in. But for some time I could find none. At last I saw what looked like a narrow gap, like a little doorway in the wall, and I tried to pass through it. But the passage was very tight and narrow, and I made many attempts to get in, all in vain, until I was almost completely worn out with struggling to get in. At last, with great struggling, I seemed first to get my head in, and after that, by squeezing sideways, my shoulders and my whole body. Then I was extremely glad, and went and sat down in the middle of them, and so was comforted with the light and heat of their sun.

55. Now this mountain and wall and the rest were explained to me like this. The mountain meant the church of the living God. The sun that shone on it meant the comforting shining of His merciful face on those who were in it. The wall, I thought, was the Word, which separates Christians from the world. And the gap in this wall, I thought, was Jesus Christ, who is the way to God the Father (John 14:6; Matt. 7:14). But because the passage was so amazingly narrow, so narrow that I could only get through it with great difficulty, it showed me that no one could enter into life except those who were in deadly earnest, and only if they left this wicked world behind them. For there was room only for body and soul, but not for body and soul and sin.

56. This picture stayed on my spirit for many days. All that time I saw myself in a lost and sad condition, yet I was stirred to an intense hunger and longing to be one of that company that sat in the sunshine. Now too I would pray wherever I was, at home or away, in the house or in the field, and with my heart lifted up I would often sing those words of the 51st Psalm, ‘O Lord, consider my distress’; for as yet I did not know where I stood.

57. Still I could not reach any comforting assurance that I had faith in Christ. Instead of finding satisfaction, I now began to find my soul attacked with fresh doubts about my future happiness, especially doubts like these: Was I elected? But what if the day of grace was now past and gone?

58. I was greatly troubled and disturbed by these two temptations, sometimes by one and sometimes by the other. To speak first of my questioning about election: I found at this time that although I was on fire to find the way to heaven and glory, and nothing could drive me off it, yet this question so upset and discouraged me that at certain times especially it was as if the very strength of my body had been taken away by its force and power. This Scripture also seemed to trample on all my desires: ‘It is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy’ (Rom. 9:16).

59. I did not know what to do with this Scripture. For I saw plainly that unless the great God, of His infinite grace and generosity, had freely chosen me to be a vessel of mercy, then though I should desire and long and labour until my heart broke, no good could come of it. So this kept sticking with me: How can you tell that you are elected? And what if you are not? What then?

60. O Lord, I thought, what if I really am not? Perhaps you are not, said the tempter. Perhaps so, indeed, I thought. Why, then, said Satan, you might as well give up and strive no further. For if you really are not elected and chosen by God, there is no point talking about your being saved; ‘For it is neither of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.’

61. These things drove me to my wits’ end, not knowing what to say or how to answer these temptations. Indeed, I hardly suspected that it was Satan attacking me like this. I thought rather that it was my own good sense raising the question. For that only the elect attain eternal life, I accepted wholeheartedly and without hesitation. But whether I myself was one of them, that was the whole question.

62. So for several days I was heavily attacked and perplexed, and often, as I walked along, I was ready to sink where I stood with faintness of mind. But one day, after I had been oppressed and cast down by this for many weeks, and was now quite giving up all my hopes of ever attaining life, this sentence fell with weight on my spirit: ‘Look at the generations of old and see; did ever any trust in the Lord, and was confounded?’

63. At this I was greatly relieved and encouraged in my soul. For at that very moment it was explained to me like this: Begin at the beginning of Genesis and read to the end of Revelation, and see whether you can find that anyone ever trusted in the Lord and was put to shame. So when I got home I went straight to my Bible to see if I could find that saying, never doubting that I would find it at once. It was so fresh in me, with such strength and comfort on my spirit, that it was as if it were talking to me.

64. Well, I looked, but I did not find it. Still it stayed with me. Then I asked first one good man and then another if they knew where it was, but they knew of no such place. At this I wondered that such a sentence should seize my heart so suddenly and with such comfort and strength, and stay there, and yet no one could find it, for I did not doubt that it was in Holy Scripture.

65. I carried on like this for more than a year and could not find the place. But at last, glancing into the books of the Apocrypha, I found it in Ecclesiasticus 2:10. At first this rather dismayed me. But because by this time I had more experience of the love and kindness of God, it troubled me less, especially when I considered that although it was not in the texts we call holy and canonical, this sentence was the sum and substance of many of the promises, and so it was my duty to take comfort from it. I bless God for that word, for it was from God to me. That word still shines before my face at times.

66. After this, that other doubt came on me with force: But what if the day of grace should be past and gone? What if you have let the time of mercy slip by? I remember that one day, as I was walking into the country, I was thinking hard about this: But what if the day of grace is past? And to make my trouble worse, the tempter brought to my mind those good people of Bedford and suggested to me that, since they were already converted, they were all that God would save in those parts, and that I had come too late, for they had received the blessing before I came.

67. Now I was in great distress, thinking that this might very well be true. So I went about lamenting my sad condition, counting myself far worse than a thousand fools for holding back so long and spending so many years in sin as I had. I kept crying out, Oh, if only I had turned sooner! Oh, if only I had turned seven years ago! It also made me angry with myself to think that I had had no more sense than to waste my time until my soul and heaven were lost.

68. But when I had been tormented by this fear for a long time and could hardly take one more step, just about the same place where I had received my other encouragement, these words broke in on my mind: ‘Compel them to come in, that my house may be filled’; ‘and yet there is room’ (Luke 14:22-23). These words, and especially ‘And yet there is room’, were sweet words to me. For truly, I thought that by them I saw there was room enough in heaven for me. And more than that, I thought that when the Lord Jesus spoke these words He was thinking of me. Knowing that the time would come when I would be troubled with fear that there was no room left for me in His heart, He spoke this word beforehand and left it on record, so that I might find help in it against this vile temptation. This is what I firmly believed at the time.

69. I went on for quite a while in the light and encouragement of this word. The comfort was all the greater when I thought that the Lord Jesus had thought of me so long ago and had spoken those words deliberately for my sake. For I truly thought then that He had spoken them on purpose to encourage me.

70. But I was not without temptations to go back again, temptations, I say, from Satan, from my own heart and from worldly acquaintances. But I thank God that these were outweighed by a sound sense of death and of the day of judgment, which stayed constantly, as it were, before my eyes. I would also often think of Nebuchadnezzar, of whom it is said that God had given him all the kingdoms of the earth (Dan. 5:19). Yet, I thought, if this great man had all his portion in this world, one hour in hell fire would make him forget it all. This thought was a great help to me.

71. About this time I was almost brought to see something about the animals that Moses counted clean and unclean. I thought those animals were pictures of people: the clean ones pictures of those who were the people of God, and the unclean ones pictures of those who were the children of the wicked one. Now I read that the clean animals chewed the cud. That, I thought, shows us we must feed on the Word of God. They also had divided hooves. I thought that meant we must part with the ways of ungodly people if we want to be saved. Reading further about them, I found that even if we chewed the cud like the hare, yet walked with paws like a dog, or even if we had divided hooves like the pig, yet did not chew the cud like the sheep, we were still unclean for all that. For I thought the hare was a picture of those who talk about the Word yet walk in the ways of sin, and that the pig was like someone who has given up his outward filthiness but still lacks the Word of faith, without which there could be no way of salvation, however devout a person might be (Deut. 14). After this I found, by reading the Word, that those who are to be glorified with Christ in another world must be called by Him here: called to share in His Word and righteousness, in the comforts and first fruits of His Spirit, and in a special interest in all those heavenly things that truly prepare the soul beforehand for that rest and house of glory in heaven above.

72. Here again I was completely brought to a halt, not knowing what to do, afraid that I was not called. For, I thought, if I am not called, what can do me any good? Only those who are effectually called inherit the kingdom of heaven. But oh, how I now loved the words that spoke of a Christian’s calling, as when the Lord said to one, ‘Follow me’, and to another, ‘Come after me’. And oh, I thought, if only He would say so to me too, how gladly I would run after Him!

73. I cannot now describe with what longings and breakings of soul I cried to Christ to call me. I carried on like this for a time, all on fire to be converted to Jesus Christ. At that time I also saw such glory in a converted state that I could not be content without a share in it. Gold! If it could have been bought with gold, what would I not have given for it! If I had owned the whole world, I would have given it all ten thousand times over for this, that my soul might be in a converted state.

74. How lovely in my eyes now was everyone I thought to be a converted man or woman! They shone; they walked like people who carried the great seal of heaven about with them. Oh, I saw that the lines had fallen to them in pleasant places, and they had a goodly heritage (Ps. 16:6). But what made me sick at heart was what Mark says of Christ: He went up into a mountain and called to Him whom He would, and they came to Him (Mark 3:13).

75. This Scripture made me faint and afraid, yet it lit a fire in my soul. What made me afraid was this: that Christ might have no liking for me, for He called ‘whom he would’. But oh, the glory I saw in that condition still held my heart so strongly that I could hardly read of anyone Christ called without wishing at once, If only I had been in their shoes; if only I had been born Peter; if only I had been born John; or if only I had been standing by and had heard Him when He called them, how I would have cried, O Lord, call me too. But oh, I was afraid He would not call me.

76. And truly the Lord let me go on like this for many months together and showed me nothing, either that I was already called or that I would be called later. But at last, after a long time and many groans to God that I might be made a sharer in the holy and heavenly calling, this Word came in on me: ‘I will cleanse their blood that I have not cleansed: for the Lord dwelleth in Zion’ (Joel 3:21). I thought these words were sent to encourage me to keep waiting on God, and they showed me that even if I was not converted to Christ already, the time might come when I would be truly converted.

77. About this time I began to open my mind to those poor people in Bedford and to tell them my condition. When they had heard it, they told Mr. Gifford about me, and he himself also took the opportunity to talk with me. He was willing to think well of me, though I think on little grounds. He invited me to his house, where I could hear him talk with others about God’s dealings with the soul. From all this I received still more conviction, and from that time I began to see something of the emptiness and inward wretchedness of my wicked heart, for until then I knew very little about it. But now it began to be uncovered to me, and also to produce wickedness at a rate it never had before. Now I plainly found that lusts and corruptions would push themselves out strongly within me, in wicked thoughts and desires, which I had not noticed before. My desires for heaven and life began to fail. I also found that whereas my soul had been full of longing for God, now my heart began to hanker after every foolish vanity. Indeed, my heart would not be moved to care about what was good. It began to grow careless of both my soul and heaven. It now constantly held back, both from every duty and in it, and was like a clog on a bird’s leg to stop her flying.

78. No, I thought, now I am getting worse and worse; now I am further from conversion than I ever was before. So I began to sink badly in my soul, and to let such discouragement into my heart that it laid me as low as hell. If I had been burned at the stake then, I could not have believed that Christ loved me. Alas, I could neither hear Him, nor see Him, nor feel Him, nor taste any of His things. I was driven as if by a storm. My heart would be unclean; the Canaanites would dwell in the land.

79. Sometimes I would tell my condition to God’s people. When they heard it, they would pity me and tell me about the promises. But they might as well have told me to reach the sun with my finger as to tell me to receive or rely on the promise. As soon as I tried to do it, all my sense and feeling was against me, and I saw that I had a heart that would sin and that lay under a law that would condemn.

80. These things have often made me think of the child whom his father brought to Christ, who, while he was still coming to Him, was thrown down by the devil and so torn by him that he lay and rolled about, foaming (Luke 9:42; Mark 9:20).

81. Further, in those days I would find my heart shutting itself up against the Lord and against His holy Word. I have found my unbelief putting its shoulder to the door, as it were, to keep Him out, and that even at times when I have cried with many a bitter sigh, Good Lord, break it open; Lord, break these gates of brass, and cut these bars of iron in two (Ps. 107:16). Yet this word would sometimes bring a peaceful pause into my heart: ‘I girded thee, though thou hast not known me’ (Isa. 45:5).

82. But all this while, as far as actually sinning was concerned, I was never more tender than now. I dared not take a pin or a stick, even one no bigger than a straw, for my conscience was now sore and would smart at every touch. I hardly knew how to speak my words, for fear of putting them wrongly. Oh, how carefully I went about everything I did or said! I found myself as if on a miry bog that shook if I so much as moved, and I was left there by God and Christ and the Spirit and all good things.

83. But I notice that, although I was such a great sinner before conversion, God never laid much of the guilt of my sins of ignorance on me. He only showed me that I was lost without Christ, because I had been a sinner. I saw that I needed a perfect righteousness to present me without fault before God, and that this righteousness was to be found nowhere but in the person of Jesus Christ.

84. But my original and inward pollution, that was my plague and my affliction. That, I say, was always pushing itself out within me at a dreadful rate. I felt its guilt to the point of amazement. Because of it I was more loathsome in my own eyes than a toad, and I thought I was the same in God’s eyes too. Sin and corruption, I said, would bubble out of my heart as naturally as water bubbles out of a spring. I now thought that everyone had a better heart than I had. I could have exchanged hearts with anybody. I thought no one but the devil himself could match me for inward wickedness and pollution of mind. So at the sight of my own vileness I fell deep into despair, for I concluded that the condition I was in could not exist alongside a state of grace. Surely, I thought, I am forsaken by God; surely I am given up to the devil and to a reprobate mind. I carried on like this for a long while, even for some years together.

85. While I was troubled like this with fears of my own damnation, there were two things that made me wonder. One was when I saw old people chasing after the things of this life as if they would live here for ever. The other was when I found professing Christians badly distressed and cast down when they met with outward losses, such as of a husband, wife or child. Lord, I thought, what a fuss there is about such little things as these! What seeking after worldly things by some, and what grief in others at losing them! If they labour so hard for the things of this present life and shed so many tears over them, how much more am I to be mourned, pitied and prayed for! My soul is dying; my soul is being damned. If only my soul were in a good condition, and I were sure of it, oh, how rich I would think myself, even if I were blessed with nothing but bread and water! I would count those losses only small troubles and bear them as light burdens. ‘A wounded spirit who can bear?’

86. And although I was troubled and tossed about and afflicted like this by the sight and sense and terror of my own wickedness, I was still afraid to let this sight and sense go entirely from my mind. For I found that unless guilt of conscience was removed the right way, that is, by the blood of Christ, a person grew worse rather than better by losing his trouble of mind. So if my guilt lay heavily on me, I would cry that the blood of Christ might take it away. And if it was going away without that (for the sense of sin would sometimes seem to die and disappear altogether), then I would also try to bring it back onto my heart by setting the punishment for sin in hell fire before my mind. I would cry, Lord, do not let it leave my heart except the right way, by the blood of Christ and by the application of Your mercy to my soul through Him. For this Scripture weighed heavily on me: ‘without shedding of blood is no remission’ (Heb. 9:22). What made me all the more afraid of this was that I had seen some people who, while they were under wounds of conscience, would cry and pray. But because they wanted relief from their trouble more than pardon for their sin, they did not care how they lost their guilt, as long as they got it out of their minds. So having got rid of it the wrong way, it was not sanctified to them, and they grew harder and blinder and more wicked after their trouble. This made me afraid, and made me cry to God all the more that it might not be so with me.

87. And now I was sorry that God had made me a man, for I feared I was a reprobate. I counted an unconverted man the most miserable of all creatures. Afflicted and tossed about like this over my sad condition, I counted myself alone, and more unblessed than most people.

88. Indeed, I thought it impossible that I would ever reach such goodness of heart as to thank God that He had made me a man. Man is indeed the noblest of all creatures in the visible world by creation, but by sin he has made himself the most ignoble. I envied the condition of the animals, birds, fish and so on, for they did not have a sinful nature. They were not offensive in God’s sight, and they were not going to hell fire after death. So I could have rejoiced if my condition had been like any of theirs.

89. I went on in this condition for a long while. But when the time of comfort came, I heard someone preach a sermon on these words in Song of Songs 4:1: ‘Behold thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair.’ At that time he made the two words ‘My love’ his main subject. After opening up the text a little, he drew from them these several conclusions: 1. That the Church, and so every saved soul, is Christ’s love, even when unlovely. 2. Christ’s love without a cause. 3. Christ’s love when hated by the world. 4. Christ’s love when under temptation and when feeling forsaken. 5. Christ’s love from first to last.

90. But I got nothing from what he said at the time. Only when he came to apply the fourth point, these were his words: If it is true that the saved soul is Christ’s love when under temptation and when feeling forsaken, then, poor tempted soul, when you are attacked and afflicted with temptation and with the hiding of God’s face, still think on these two words, ‘My love’.

91. So as I was going home, these words came back into my thoughts. I well remember that as I came in I said this in my heart: What will I gain by thinking about these two words? No sooner had this thought passed through my heart than the words began to kindle in my spirit like this, ‘Thou art my love, thou art my love’, twenty times over. And as they kept running through my mind like this, they grew stronger and warmer and began to make me look up. But being still between hope and fear, I kept answering in my heart, But is it true, but is it true? At this, these words fell in on me: he ‘wist not that it was true which was done by the angel’ (Acts 12:9).

92. Then I began to give way to the word, which with power made this joyful sound in my soul over and over again: You are my love, you are my love, and nothing shall separate you from my love. With that, Romans 8:39 came into my mind. Now my heart was filled full of comfort and hope, and now I could believe that my sins would be forgiven me. Indeed, I was now so overcome by the love and mercy of God that I remember I did not know how to contain myself until I got home. I thought I could have spoken of His love and His mercy to me even to the crows sitting on the ploughed fields in front of me, if they had been able to understand me. So I said in my soul with great gladness, Well, I wish I had a pen and ink here; I would write this down before I go any further, for surely I will not forget this forty years from now. But alas, within less than forty days I began to question it all again, which made me go on questioning everything.

93. Yet at times I was still helped to believe that it had been a true showing of grace to my soul, though I had lost much of its life and sweetness. About a week or two after this, I was strongly pursued by this Scripture: ‘Simon, Simon, behold Satan hath desired to have you’ (Luke 22:31). Sometimes it would sound so loudly within me, and as it were call after me so strongly, that once, more than all the other times, I turned my head over my shoulder, really thinking that some man behind me had called to me. It seemed to me that he called so loudly from a great distance. As I have thought since, it came to stir me up to prayer and watchfulness. It came to warn me that a cloud and a storm were coming down on me, but I did not understand it.

94. As I remember, the time it called to me so loudly was the last time it sounded in my ear. But I seem to hear still with what a loud voice these words, Simon, Simon, sounded in my ears. As I have told you, I really thought that someone half a mile behind me had called after me. And although that was not my name, it made me suddenly look behind me, believing that the one who called so loudly meant me.

95. But I was so foolish and ignorant that I did not know the reason for this sound. As I both saw and felt soon afterwards, it was sent from heaven as an alarm, to wake me up to prepare for what was coming. It only made me ponder and wonder in my mind what the reason could be that this Scripture should keep sounding and rattling in my ears so often and so loudly. But, as I said before, I soon afterwards saw God’s purpose in it.

96. For about a month later a very great storm came down on me, which treated me twenty times worse than everything I had met with before. It came creeping up on me, first one piece and then another. First all my comfort was taken from me. Then darkness seized me. After that, whole floods of blasphemies, against God, Christ and the Scriptures, were poured onto my spirit, to my great confusion and astonishment. These blasphemous thoughts also stirred up questions in me against the very existence of God and of His only beloved Son: whether there really was a God or a Christ or not, and whether the holy Scriptures were not a fable and a cleverly made-up story rather than the holy and pure Word of God.

97. The tempter would also attack me hard with this: How can you tell that the Turks do not have as good Scriptures to prove their Muhammad the Saviour as we have to prove our Jesus is? And could I believe that so many tens of thousands, in so many countries and kingdoms, should be without the knowledge of the right way to heaven, if there really is a heaven, and that we alone, who live in a corner of the earth, should be blessed with it? Everyone thinks his own religion is the right one, Jews and Moors and pagans alike. And what if all our faith, and Christ, and Scriptures, should be only a matter of opinion too?

98. Sometimes I tried to argue against these suggestions and to set some of the sayings of blessed Paul against them. But alas, as soon as I did this, I felt arguments like these coming back at me: Though we made so much of Paul and his words, how could I tell that he was not in fact a subtle and cunning man who gave himself up to deceive with strong delusions, and who took all that trouble and toil to ruin and destroy his fellows?

99. These suggestions, with many others which at this time I may not and dare not utter, either in speech or in writing, took such a hold on my spirit, and so weighed down my heart by their number, persistence and fiery force, that I felt as if there was nothing else in me from morning to night but these, and as if there could be room for nothing else. I also concluded that God, in real anger against my soul, had given me up to them, to be carried away by them as by a mighty whirlwind.

100. Only by the distaste they caused my spirit did I feel that there was something in me that refused to embrace them. But I had this thought only when God gave me a moment’s breathing space. Otherwise the noise and strength and force of these temptations would drown and overflow, and as it were bury, all such thoughts and every memory of anything of the kind. While I was in this temptation, I would often find my mind suddenly pushed to curse and swear, or to say something grievous against God, or Christ His Son, or the Scriptures.

101. Now I thought, surely I am possessed by the devil. At other times I thought I would lose my mind. For instead of praising and magnifying God the Lord with others, if I so much as heard Him spoken of, at once some horrible blasphemous thought or other would shoot out of my heart against Him. So whether I thought that God existed or thought again that there was no such thing, I could feel no love, no peace and no gracious disposition within me.

102. These things sank me into very deep despair, for I concluded that such things could not possibly be found among those who loved God. Often, when these temptations were heavy on me, I compared myself to a child whom some gipsy has snatched up by force under her apron and is carrying away from friends and country. I did kick sometimes, and scream and cry, but I was still as if bound in the wings of the temptation, and the wind would carry me away. I thought also of Saul and of the evil spirit that possessed him, and I greatly feared that my condition was the same as his (1 Sam. 16:14).

103. In those days, when I heard others talk about what the sin against the Holy Spirit was, the tempter would so provoke me to want to commit that sin that it was as if I could not, must not and would not be quiet until I had committed it. Now no sin would do but that one. If it was to be committed by speaking a certain word, then it was as if my mouth would speak that word whether I wanted to or not. This temptation was so strong on me that I have often been ready to clap my hand under my chin to keep my mouth from opening. With the same aim I have at other times thought of throwing myself head first into some dung-heap hole or other, to keep my mouth from speaking.

104. Now I envied the condition of the dog and the toad, and counted the state of everything God had made far better than this dreadful state of mine and of those like me. Indeed, I would gladly have been in the condition of a dog or a horse, for I knew they had no soul to perish under the everlasting weights of hell for sin, as mine was likely to do. And though I saw this and felt this and was broken to pieces by it, what added to my sorrow was that I could not find that I desired deliverance with all my soul. In the middle of these torments, that Scripture also tore my soul apart: ‘The wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire and dirt. There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked.’

105. And now my heart was at times extremely hard. If I had been willing to give a thousand pounds for a tear, I could not have shed one; no, sometimes I could hardly even want to shed one. I was very downcast to think that this should be my lot. I saw that some could mourn and lament their sin, that others could rejoice and bless God for Christ, and others again could talk quietly about the Word of God and remember it with gladness, while I alone was in the storm. This sank me deeply. I thought I was alone in my condition. So I would bewail my hard luck greatly, but I could not get out of these things or get rid of them.

106. While this temptation lasted, which was about a year, I could not take part in any of God’s ordinances without severe and great affliction. Indeed, it was then that I was most distressed with blasphemies. If I was hearing the Word, uncleanness, blasphemies and despair would hold me captive there. If I was reading, then sometimes I had sudden thoughts questioning everything I read. At other times my mind would be so strangely snatched away and taken up with other things that I neither knew nor noticed nor remembered even the sentence I had just read.

107. I was also greatly troubled in prayer at this time. Sometimes I thought I would see the devil. Indeed, I thought I could feel him behind me pulling at my clothes. He was also constantly at me during prayer to get it over with: break off, hurry up, you have prayed enough, stay no longer, always drawing my mind away. Sometimes too he would throw in wicked thoughts like these: that I must pray to him, or for him. I have sometimes thought of these words, Fall down, or, ‘if thou wilt fall down and worship me’ (Matt. 4:9).

108. Also, when I had wandering thoughts during this duty and tried hard to compose my mind and fix it on God, the tempter worked with great force to distract and confuse me and turn my mind away, by presenting to my heart and imagination the shape of a bush, a bull, a broom or the like, as if I should pray to them. At some times especially he would hold my mind on these things so strongly that it was as if I could think of nothing else and pray to nothing else but these, or things like them.

109. Yet at times I had some strong and heart-moving sense of God and of the reality of the truth of His gospel. But oh, how my heart would pour itself out at such times with groanings that cannot be put into words! My whole soul was then in every word. I would cry out with pangs to God that He would be merciful to me. But then I would be dismayed again by fancies like these: I would think that God was mocking these prayers of mine, saying, and that in the hearing of the holy angels, This poor simple wretch hankers after Me as if I had nothing to do with My mercy but give it to people like him. Alas, poor fool, how you are deceived! It is not for people like you to have favour with the Most High.

110. Then the tempter also came at me with discouragements like these: You are very eager for mercy, but I will cool you down. This frame of mind will not last for ever. Many have been as eager as you for the Spirit, but I have quenched their zeal. And with this, various people who had fallen away would be set before my eyes. Then I would be afraid that I would do the same. But, I thought, I am glad this has come into my mind. Well, I will keep watch and take all the care I can. Even if you do, said Satan, I will be too strong for you. I will cool you without your noticing, by degrees, little by little. What do I care, he said, if I take seven years to chill your heart, as long as I can do it in the end? Constant rocking will lull a crying child to sleep. I will keep at it, but I will get what I want. Though you are burning hot now, if I can pull you away from this fire, I will have you cold before long.

111. These things put me in great difficulty. For just as I could not find myself ready to die now, so I thought that living long would make me even less ready. For time would make me forget everything, and wear even the memory of the evil of sin, the worth of heaven and my need of the blood of Christ to wash me, out of my mind and thoughts. But I thank Christ Jesus that for the present these things did not make me slacken my crying out, but rather pushed me to it all the more, like the woman who met with the adulterer (Deut. 22:27). In those days, after I had suffered these things for a while, this was a good word to me: ‘I am persuaded that neither height, nor depth, nor life,’ etc., ‘shall separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus’ (Rom. 8:38). And now I hoped that a long life would not destroy me or make me miss heaven.

112. Yet I had some supports in this temptation, though at the time I questioned them all. The beginning of the third chapter of Jeremiah meant something to me, and so did the thought of the fifth verse of that chapter: that though we have spoken and done all the evil we could, we should still cry to God, ‘My Father, Thou art the guide of my youth’, and should return to Him.

113. I also once had a sweet glimpse from 2 Corinthians 5:21: ‘For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.’ I remember too that one day, as I was sitting in a neighbour’s house, very sad at the thought of my many blasphemies, and was saying in my mind, What grounds do I have to think that I, who have been so vile and abominable, should ever inherit eternal life? this word came suddenly on me: ‘What shall we then say to these things? If God be for us, who can be against us?’ (Rom. 8:31). This too was a help to me: ‘Because I live, ye shall live also’ (John 14:19). But these were only hints, touches and short visits, though very sweet while they lasted. They did not last, but like Peter’s sheet, they were suddenly taken up from me into heaven again (Acts 10:16).

114. But afterwards the Lord revealed Himself to me more fully and graciously. Indeed, He completely delivered me, not only from the guilt that these things had laid on my conscience, but also from their very filth. For the temptation was removed, and I was put back into my right mind, as other Christians were.

115. I remember that one day, as I was travelling into the country, brooding on the wickedness and blasphemy of my heart and thinking about the hostility to God that was in me, this Scripture came into my mind: He hath ‘made peace through the blood of his cross’ (Col. 1:20). Through it I was made to see again and again and again that day that God and my soul were friends through this blood. Indeed, I saw that the justice of God and my sinful soul could embrace and kiss each other through this blood. This was a good day for me; I hope I will not forget it.

116. Another time, as I sat by the fire in my house brooding on my wretchedness, the Lord made this too a precious word to me: ‘Forasmuch, then, as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver them who, through fear of death, were all their lifetime subject to bondage’ (Heb. 2:14-15). I thought the glory of these words weighed on me so heavily then that once or twice I was ready to faint where I sat, yet not with grief and trouble, but with solid joy and peace.

117. At this time I was also sitting under the ministry of holy Mr. Gifford, whose teaching, by God’s grace, did much to steady me. This man made it his main business to deliver God’s people from all the faults and unsound resting places that by nature we are inclined to take up and make for our souls.
