He urged us to take special care not to take any truth on trust, from this man or that man or any other people, but to cry mightily to God that He would convince us of its reality and settle us in it by His own Spirit through the holy Word. For, he said, if you do otherwise, when temptations come, if they come strongly, you will find, not having received these truths with evidence from heaven, that you lack the help and strength to resist that you once thought you had.

118. This was as timely for my soul as the early and the late rain in their season. For I had found the truth of his words, and that by sad experience. I had felt that no one can say that Jesus Christ is Lord except by the Holy Spirit, especially when tempted by the devil. So I found my soul, through grace, very ready to drink in this teaching, and inclined to pray to God that in nothing that concerned God’s glory and my own eternal happiness He would leave me without its confirmation from heaven. For now I saw clearly that there was a huge difference between the notions of flesh and blood and the revelations of God in heaven, and also a great difference between a faith that is pretended and rests on human wisdom, and the faith that comes from a person’s being born to it by God (Matt. 16:15-17; 1 John 5:1).

119. But oh, how my soul was now led by God from truth to truth, even from the birth and cradle of the Son of God to His ascension and His second coming from heaven to judge the world!

120. Truly, I found then that the great God was very good to me in this respect. For as far as I remember, there was nothing I cried to God to make known and reveal to me that He was not pleased to do for me. I mean that there was not one part of the gospel of the Lord Jesus into which I was not led in due order. It seemed to me that I saw with great clearness, from the accounts of the four evangelists, the wonderful work of God in giving Jesus Christ to save us, from His conception and birth right through to His second coming to judgment. It seemed as if I had seen Him born, as if I had seen Him grow up, as if I had seen Him walk through this world from the cradle to His cross. And when He came to the cross, I saw how gently He gave Himself to be hung and nailed on it for my sins and wicked deeds. Also, as I was thinking about this course of His, these words dropped on my spirit: He was ordained for the slaughter (1 Pet. 1:19-20).

121. When I have also thought about the truth of His resurrection, and remembered the words ‘Touch me not, Mary,’ etc., it was as if I saw Him leap at the mouth of the grave for joy that He had risen again and had won the victory over our dreadful enemies (John 20:17). I have also seen Him in the spirit, a man at the right hand of God the Father for me, and have seen the manner of His coming from heaven to judge the world in glory. I was confirmed in these things by the following Scriptures: Acts 1:9-10; 7:56; 10:42; Heb. 7:24; 8:3; Rev. 1:18; 1 Thess. 4:17-18.

122. Once I was greatly troubled to know whether the Lord Jesus was man as well as God, and God as well as man. And truly, in those days, whatever people said, unless I had it with evidence from heaven it was all as nothing to me; I did not count myself settled in any truth of God. Well, I was greatly troubled about this point and did not know how to settle it. At last the words in the fifth chapter of Revelation came into my mind: ‘And I beheld, and lo, in the midst of the throne and of the four beasts, and in the midst of the elders, stood a Lamb.’ In the midst of the throne, I thought, there is His Godhead; in the midst of the elders, there is His manhood. And oh, it seemed to me that this sparkled! It was a fine touch and gave me sweet satisfaction. Another Scripture also helped me a great deal in this: ‘To us a child is born, unto us a son is given; and the government shall be on his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace,’ etc. (Isa. 9:6).

123. Besides these teachings of God in His Word, the Lord also used two things to confirm me in these matters. One was the errors of the Quakers, and the other was the guilt of sin. For as the Quakers opposed His truth, God confirmed me in it all the more, by leading me into the Scriptures that wonderfully upheld it.

124. The errors that this group held at that time were these: 1. That the holy Scriptures were not the Word of God. 2. That every person in the world had the Spirit of Christ, grace, faith and so on. 3. That Christ Jesus, crucified and dying 1600 years ago, did not satisfy divine justice for the sins of the people. 4. That Christ’s flesh and blood was within the saints. 5. That the bodies of the good and the bad that are buried in the churchyard will not rise again. 6. That the resurrection has already taken place for good people. 7. That the man Jesus, who was crucified between two thieves on Mount Calvary in the land of Canaan near Jerusalem, had not ascended above the starry heavens. 8. That He, the very same Jesus who died at the hands of the Jews, would not come again on the last day and as man judge all nations, and so on.

125. Many more vile and abominable things were stirred up by them in those days. Through these I was driven to search the Scriptures more closely, and through their light and testimony I was not only enlightened but greatly confirmed and comforted in the truth. And, as I said, the guilt of sin helped me a great deal. For whenever it came on me, the blood of Christ took it away again, and again, and again, and that sweetly, according to the Scriptures. O friends, cry to God to reveal Jesus Christ to you; there is no one who teaches like Him.

126. It would take too long for me to stop here and tell you in detail how God settled me in all the things of Christ, and how, in order to do so, He led me into His words. I would also have to tell how He opened them to me, made them shine before me, and comforted me over and over again, about His own being and the being of His Son, and Spirit, and Word, and gospel.

127. I will only say to you again what I said before: that in general He was pleased to deal with me in this way. First He let me be afflicted with temptation about these things, and then He revealed them to me. For example, sometimes I would lie under great guilt for sin, even crushed to the ground by it, and then the Lord would show me the death of Christ. Indeed, He would so sprinkle my conscience with His blood that I would find, and that before I knew it, that in the very conscience where the law had just been reigning and raging, the peace and love of God through Christ would rest and remain.

128. Now I had, as I thought, evidence of my salvation from heaven, with many golden seals on it, all hanging in my sight. Now I could remember this showing and that discovery of grace with comfort. I would often long and wish that the last day had come, so that I might be set on fire for ever with the sight of Him, the joy of Him, and fellowship with Him whose head was crowned with thorns, whose face was spat on, whose body was broken and whose soul was made an offering for my sins. For whereas before I had lain constantly trembling at the mouth of hell, now it seemed to me I had got so far from it that when I looked back I could hardly make it out. And oh, I thought, if only I were eighty years old now, so that I might die quickly and my soul might be gone to rest.

129. But before I had got this far out of my temptations, I greatly longed to see the experience of some godly man of long ago, who had written some hundreds of years before I was born. For as for those who had written in our own day, I thought (but I ask them now to forgive me) that they had written only what others felt, or else had studied, through the strength of their intelligence and abilities, to answer the objections they saw others were troubled by, without going down into the depths themselves. Well, after many such longings in my mind, the God in whose hands are all our days and ways one day put into my hand a book by Martin Luther. It was his commentary on Galatians, and it was so old that it was ready to fall apart if I so much as turned it over. I was very pleased that such an old book had come into my hands. When I had read only a little of it, I found my own condition dealt with in his experience so fully and so deeply that it was as if his book had been written out of my heart. This amazed me, for I thought, This man could not know anything of the state of Christians now, but must be writing and speaking of the experience of former days.

130. Besides this, in that book he also discusses very seriously how these temptations arise, namely blasphemy, despair and the like, showing that the law of Moses, as well as the devil, death and hell, has a very great part in them. At first this was very strange to me, but as I thought about it and watched, I found that it was indeed so. I do not intend to go into particulars here. Only this, I think, I must declare before everyone: I prefer this book of Martin Luther on Galatians, apart from the Holy Bible, before all the books I have ever seen, as the most fitting for a wounded conscience.

131. And now I found, as I thought, that I loved Christ dearly. Oh, it seemed to me that my soul clung to Him, my affections clung to Him; I felt love for Him as hot as fire. And now, as Job said, I thought I would die in my nest. But I quickly found that my great love was only small, and that I, who had, as I thought, such burning love for Jesus Christ, could let Him go again for a mere trifle. God knows how to humble us and can hide pride from man. Soon after this my love was thoroughly tested.

132. For after the Lord had graciously delivered me in this way from that great and severe temptation, had settled me so sweetly in the faith of His holy gospel, and had given me such strong comfort and blessed evidence from heaven about my share in His love through Christ, the tempter came at me again, and with a more grievous and dreadful temptation than before.

133. It was this: to sell and part with this most blessed Christ, to exchange Him for the things of this life, for anything at all. The temptation lay on me for about a year and followed me so constantly that I was not free of it one day in a month, and sometimes not even for one hour in many days together, except when I was asleep.

134. In my judgment I was persuaded that those who were once truly in Christ, as I hoped through His grace I had seen myself to be, could never lose Him for ever, for ‘the land shall not be sold for ever, for the land is mine,’ says God (Lev. 25:23). Yet it was a constant torment to me to think that I should have even one such thought within me against a Christ, a Jesus, who had done for me what He had done. And yet at that time I had almost no other thoughts but blasphemous ones like these.

135. But neither my dislike of the thought, nor any desire or effort to resist it, in the least shook or lessened its persistence, or its force and strength. For it mixed itself with almost everything I thought, in such a way that I could not eat my food, bend down for a pin, chop a stick or glance at this or that, without the temptation coming: Sell Christ for this, or sell Christ for that; sell Him, sell Him.

136. Sometimes it would run through my thoughts no fewer than a hundred times over, Sell Him, sell Him, sell Him. Against it I can say that for whole hours at a time I was forced to stand constantly leaning and straining my spirit against it, in case some wicked thought might arise in my heart before I knew it and consent to it. And sometimes the tempter would make me believe I had consented to it, and then I would be as if tortured on a rack for whole days together.

137. This temptation put me in such fear that at some time, I say, I might consent to it and be overcome by it, that through the sheer force of my mind straining to contradict and resist this wickedness, even my body would be set in action or motion, pushing or thrusting with my hands or elbows. I kept answering as fast as the destroyer said, Sell Him: I will not, I will not, I will not, I will not; no, not for thousands, thousands, thousands of worlds. I reckoned like this in case, in the middle of these attacks, I should value Him too low, until I hardly knew where I was or how to calm myself again.

138. At these times he would not let me eat my food in peace. No, indeed, when I was sitting at the table at my meal, I must go off to pray. I must leave my food now, this very minute, so counterfeit holy would this devil be. When I was tempted like this, I would say to myself, I am at my meal now; let me finish it. No, he said, you must do it now, or you will displease God and despise Christ. So I was greatly afflicted by these things. And because of the sinfulness of my nature, imagining that these things were promptings from God, I would refuse to do it, as if I were refusing God. And then I would feel as guilty for not obeying a temptation of the devil as if I had really broken the law of God.

139. But to be brief: one morning, as I lay in bed, I was attacked most fiercely, as at other times, with this temptation to sell and part with Christ. The wicked suggestion kept running through my mind, Sell Him, sell Him, sell Him, sell Him, sell Him, as fast as a person could speak. And as at other times I answered it in my mind, No, no, not for thousands, thousands, thousands, at least twenty times over. But at last, after much struggling, until I was almost out of breath, I felt this thought pass through my heart: Let Him go, if He will! And I thought also that I felt my heart freely consent to it. Oh, the diligence of Satan! Oh, the desperate state of the human heart!

140. Now the battle was won, and down I fell, like a bird shot from the top of a tree, into great guilt and fearful despair. Getting out of bed, I went moping into the field, but God knows with as heavy a heart as I think any mortal could bear. There for about two hours I was like a man deprived of life, as if now past all recovery and bound over to eternal punishment.

141. And along with this, this Scripture seized my soul: ‘Or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat, sold his birthright; for ye know, how that afterward, when he would have inherited the blessing, he was rejected; for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears’ (Heb. 12:16-17).

142. Now I was like someone in chains. I felt myself shut up to the judgment to come. For two years together nothing would stay with me but damnation and the expectation of damnation. I say, nothing would stay with me now but this, apart from a few moments of relief, as you will see in what follows.

143. These words were to my soul like fetters of brass on my legs, and I went about for several months together with their sound constantly in my ears. But one day about ten or eleven o’clock, as I was walking under a hedge, full of sorrow and guilt, God knows, and lamenting my hard luck that such a thought should arise within me, this sentence suddenly burst in on me: The blood of Christ remits all guilt. At this I came to a stop in my spirit. With that, this word took hold of me: ‘The blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanseth us from all sin’ (1 John 1:7).

144. Now I began to feel peace in my soul, and it seemed to me that I saw the tempter leer and slink away from me, as if ashamed of what he had done. At the same time my sin and the blood of Christ were shown to me like this: that my sin, compared with the blood of Christ, was no more than this little clod or stone in front of me is to the vast, wide field I see here. This gave me good encouragement for two or three hours, and during that time it seemed to me also that I saw by faith the Son of God suffering for my sins. But because it did not last, I sank again in my spirit under extreme guilt.

145. It was chiefly because of the Scripture I mentioned before, about Esau selling his birthright. For that Scripture would lie in my mind all day long, all week long, indeed all year long, and hold me down so that I could not lift myself up at all. For whenever I tried to turn to this Scripture or that for relief, that sentence would still be sounding in me: ‘For ye know, how that afterward, when he would have inherited the blessing—he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.’

146. Sometimes I would also feel a touch from the words in Luke 22:32, ‘I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not’. But it would not stay with me. Nor indeed, when I considered my state, could I find the least ground for thinking that the root of that grace could be in me, having sinned as I had. Now I was torn apart and in a sorry state for many days together.

147. Then with a sad and anxious heart I began to consider the nature and extent of my sin, and to search the Word of God to see whether I could spot a word of promise anywhere, or any encouraging sentence from which I might take relief. So I began to consider the third chapter of Mark: All manner of sins and blasphemies shall be forgiven unto the sons of men, wherewith soever they shall blaspheme. At first sight it seemed to me that this place contained a broad and glorious promise of pardon for great offences. But considering the place more fully, I thought it was rather to be understood as referring chiefly to those who had done the things mentioned there while in their natural state, and not to me, who had not only received light and mercy, but had afterwards, and in spite of that, treated Christ with such contempt as I had.

148. So I feared that this wicked sin of mine might be the unpardonable sin, of which He speaks there: ‘But he that shall blaspheme against the Holy Ghost hath never forgiveness, but is in danger of eternal damnation’ (Mark 3:29). And I believed this all the more because of that sentence in Hebrews: ‘For ye know, how that afterward, when he would have inherited the blessing, he was rejected; for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.’ And this always stuck with me.

149. Now I was both a burden and a terror to myself. Never before had I known as I did now what it was to be weary of life and yet afraid to die. Oh, how gladly I would have been anybody but myself, anything but a man, and in any condition but my own! For nothing passed through my mind more often than that it was impossible for my sin to be forgiven and for me to be saved from the wrath to come.

150. And now I began to strain to call back the time that was past, wishing two thousand times over that the day when I would be tempted to such a sin had still not come. I concluded with great indignation, against both my heart and all the attacks, that I would rather have been torn to pieces than be found consenting to it. But alas, these thoughts and wishes and resolutions were now too late to help me. The thought had passed through my heart; God had let me go, and I had fallen. Oh, I thought, ‘that it was with me as in months past, as in the days when God preserved me!’ (Job 29:2).

151. Then again, being reluctant and unwilling to perish, I began to compare my sin with other people’s, to see whether I could find that any of those who were saved had done what I had done. So I considered David’s adultery and murder, and found them most terrible crimes, and committed after he had received light and grace too. Yet on reflection I saw that his sins were only against the law of Moses, from which the Lord Christ could deliver him with the consent of His Word. But mine was against the gospel, indeed against its Mediator. I had sold my Saviour.

152. Now again I would be as if stretched on the wheel, when I considered that besides the guilt that held me, I should be so empty of grace, so bewitched. What, I thought, must it be this sin and no other? Must it be the great transgression (Ps. 19:13)? Must that wicked one touch my soul (1 John 5:18)? Oh, what stings I found in all these sayings!

153. What, I thought, is there only one sin that is unpardonable, only one sin that puts the soul beyond the reach of God’s mercy, and must I be guilty of that? Must it be that one? Is there only one sin among so many millions of sins for which there is no forgiveness, and must I commit it? Oh, unhappy sin! Oh, unhappy man! These things would so break and confuse my spirit that I did not know what to do. At times I thought they would drive me out of my mind. And still, to make my misery worse, this would run through my mind: ‘Ye know how that afterward, when he would have inherited the blessing, he was rejected.’ Oh, no one knows the terrors of those days but me.

154. After this I came to consider Peter’s sin, which he committed in denying his Master. Of all the sins I could find, this indeed came closest to mine. For he had denied his Saviour, as I had, and that after receiving light and mercy, and after being warned too. I also considered that he did it once and again, and with time to think in between. But though I put all these circumstances together, so that if possible I might find help, I considered again that his was only a denial of his Master, while mine was a selling of my Saviour. So I thought to myself that I came nearer to Judas than to either David or Peter.

155. Here again my torment would flare up and afflict me. Indeed, it would grind me to powder, as it were, to see how God preserved others while I fell into the snare. For in considering other people’s sins like this and comparing them with my own, I could see plainly how God preserved them in spite of their wickedness, and would not let them become sons of perdition, as He had let me.

156. But oh, how my soul valued at this time the protection that God set around His people! Ah, how safely I saw them walk, whom God had hedged in! They were within His care, protection and special providence. Though by nature they were every bit as bad as I was, yet because He loved them He would not let them fall outside the range of mercy. But as for me, I was gone; I had done it. He would not preserve me or keep me, but because I was a reprobate He let me fall as I had. Now those blessed passages that spoke of God’s keeping His people shone like the sun before me, though not to comfort me, but to show me the blessed state and inheritance of those whom the Lord had blessed.

157. Now I saw that just as God had His hand in all the providences and dealings that came on His elect, so He had His hand in all the temptations they had to sin against Him. He did this not to stir them up to wickedness, but to choose their temptations and troubles for them, and also to leave them for a time only to such sins as would not destroy them but humble them, sins that would not put them beyond the renewing of His mercy but lay them in its way. But oh, what love, what care, what kindness and mercy I now saw mixed with the most severe and dreadful of all God’s ways with His people! He would let David, Hezekiah, Solomon, Peter and others fall, but He would not let them fall into the unpardonable sin, or into hell for sin. Oh, I thought, these are the men God has loved; these are the men whom God keeps safe beside Him even while He disciplines them, and whom He makes to dwell under the shadow of the Almighty. But all these thoughts added sorrow, grief and horror to me, for whatever I now thought about was killing to me. If I thought of how God kept His own, that was killing to me. If I thought of how I was falling myself, that was killing to me. Just as all things worked together for the best and for the good of those who were called according to His purpose, so I thought that all things worked for my harm and for my eternal ruin.

158. Then again I began to compare my sin with the sin of Judas, so that if possible I might find that mine was different from the one that is truly unpardonable. And oh, I thought, if it should differ from it by even the breadth of a hair, what a happy condition my soul is in! On consideration I found that Judas did his deliberately, but mine was against my prayers and struggles. Besides, his was committed with much forethought, but mine in a fearful hurry, all of a sudden. All this while I was tossed to and fro like the locusts, and driven from trouble to sorrow, always hearing in my ears the sound of Esau’s fall and of its dreadful consequences.

159. Yet this consideration about Judas and his sin was for a while some small relief to me, for I saw that, as far as the circumstances went, I had not sinned as foully as he had. But this was quickly gone again. For I thought to myself that there might be more than one way to commit the unpardonable sin, and that there might be degrees of it as well as of other sins. So, for all I could see yet, this sin of mine might be one that could never be passed over.

160. I was often ashamed now that I should be like such an ugly man as Judas. I also thought how loathsome I would be to all the saints on the day of judgment. So much so that I could now hardly see a good man whom I believed to have a good conscience without feeling my heart tremble at him while I was with him. Oh, now I saw a glory in walking with God, and what a mercy it was to have a good conscience before Him.

161. About this time I was strongly tempted to comfort myself by accepting some false opinion, such as that there would be no day of judgment, that we would not rise again, and that sin was not such a grievous thing. The tempter suggested this to me: Even if these things should really be true, believing otherwise would give you ease for now. If you must perish, do not torment yourself so much beforehand. Drive the thoughts of damnation out of your mind by filling it with some of the conclusions that atheists and Ranters use to help themselves.

162. But oh, when such thoughts passed through my heart, how death and judgment came into view, as it were, within a step! It seemed to me that the Judge stood at the door; it was as if it had come already. So such things could find no welcome. But I think I see from this that Satan will use any means to keep the soul from Christ. He does not like an awakened spirit. False security, blindness, darkness and error are the very kingdom and dwelling place of the wicked one.

163. I found it hard work now to pray to God, because despair was swallowing me up. I thought I was driven away from God as if by a storm. For whenever I cried to God for mercy, this would come in: It is too late; I am lost; God has let me fall, not to correct me but to condemn me; my sin is unpardonable; and I know about Esau, how after he had sold his birthright he wanted to receive the blessing but was rejected. About this time I came across that dreadful story of the miserable man Francis Spira, a book that was to my troubled spirit like salt rubbed into a fresh wound. Every sentence in that book, every groan of that man, and all the rest of what he did in his agony, his tears, his prayers, his gnashing of teeth, his wringing of hands, his writhing and twisting, his languishing and wasting away under the mighty hand of God that was on him, was like knives and daggers in my soul. One saying of his especially frightened me: Man knows the beginning of sin, but who sets the limits of where it ends? Then the earlier sentence, as the conclusion of everything, would fall again like a hot thunderbolt

on my conscience: ‘for you know how that afterward, when he would have inherited the blessing, he was rejected; for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.’

164. Then I was struck with a very great trembling, so much so that at times, for whole days together, I could feel my very body, as well as my mind, shake and totter under the sense of the dreadful judgment of God that would fall on those who have committed that most fearful and unpardonable sin. Because of this terror I also felt such a heaviness and burning in my stomach that at certain times especially it was as if my breastbone would split apart. Then I thought of what is said about Judas, who fell headlong, burst open in the middle, and all his bowels gushed out (Acts 1:18).

165. I also feared that this was the mark the Lord set on Cain: constant fear and trembling under the heavy load of guilt He had laid on him for the blood of his brother Abel. So I writhed and twisted and shrank under the burden that was on me. This burden weighed on me so heavily that I could neither stand nor walk nor lie down with any rest or quiet.

166. Yet this saying would sometimes come to my mind: He hath received gifts for the rebellious (Ps. 68:18). ‘The rebellious,’ I thought; why, surely they are those who were once subjects of their prince, those who swore allegiance to his government and then took up arms against him. And this, I thought, is exactly my condition. Once I loved Him, feared Him and served Him, but now I am a rebel. I have sold Him; I have said, Let Him go if He will. But still He has gifts for rebels, so why not for me?

167. I thought about this sometimes, and would try hard to take hold of it, so that I might draw some refreshment from it, however small. But in this too I missed what I wanted. I was driven past it by force. I was like a man being led to the place of execution, right past the place where he would gladly creep in and hide, but may not.

168. Again, after I had considered the sins of the saints one by one like this and found that mine went beyond them, I began to think this to myself: Suppose I put all theirs together and set mine alone against them, might I not find some encouragement then? For if mine, though bigger than any one of theirs, should be only equal to all of them together, then there is hope. For the blood that has power enough to wash away all theirs also has power enough to take away mine, even if this one is fully as big as all of theirs, if not bigger. Here again I would consider the sins of David, Solomon, Manasseh, Peter and the rest of the great offenders, and I would also try, as far as I fairly could, to make their sins worse and heavier by various circumstances. But alas, it was all in vain.

169. I would think to myself that David shed blood to cover up his adultery, and did it by the sword of the children of Ammon, a deed that could only be done by sustained and deliberate scheming, which made his sin much worse. But then this would turn back on me: Ah, but these were only sins against the law, from which a Jesus was sent to save them. Yours is a sin against the Saviour, and who will save you from that?

170. Then I thought of Solomon, and how he sinned in loving foreign women, in falling away to their idols, in building them temples, and in doing this against the light, in his old age, after receiving great mercy. But the same conclusion that cut me off in the previous case cut me off in this one: that all these were only sins against the law, for which God had provided a remedy. But I had sold my Saviour, and now there remained no more sacrifice for sin.

171. I would then add to those men’s sins the sins of Manasseh: how he built altars for idols in the house of the Lord. He also observed omens, used enchantments, dealt with wizards, was a wizard himself, kept familiar spirits, burned his children in the fire as sacrifices to devils, and made the streets of Jerusalem run with the blood of innocent people. These, I thought, are great sins, sins of a bloody colour. Yet it would turn back on me again: None of them is of the same kind as yours. You have parted with Jesus; you have sold your Saviour.

172. This one thought would always kill my heart: my sin was directly against my Saviour, and at such a height that I had said of Him in my heart, Let Him go if He will. Oh, it seemed to me that this sin was bigger than the sins of a country, of a kingdom or of the whole world. No pardonable sin, nor all of them together, could equal mine; mine outstripped every one of them.

173. Now I would find my mind fleeing from God as from the face of a dreadful judge. Yet this was my torment: I could not escape His hand. ‘It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God’ (Heb. 10:31). But blessed be His grace, in these flights of mine this Scripture would call out as if running after me: ‘I have blotted out, as a thick cloud, thy transgressions; and, as a cloud, thy sins: return unto me, for I have redeemed thee’ (Isa. 44:22). This, I say, would come into my mind when I was fleeing from the face of God. For I did flee from His face; that is, my mind and spirit fled before Him, because I could not bear His majesty. Then the text would cry, ‘Return unto me, for I have redeemed thee.’ Indeed, this would make me stop for a moment and, as it were, look back over my shoulder to see whether I could make out the God of grace following me with a pardon in His hand. But no sooner had I done that than everything would be clouded and darkened again by that sentence: ‘For you know how that afterward, when he would have inherited the blessing, he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.’ So I could not return, but fled, though at times it cried ‘Return, return’, as if it were shouting after me. But I was afraid to accept it, in case it did not come from God. For that other text, as I said, was still sounding in my conscience: ‘For you know how that afterward, when he would have inherited the blessing, he was rejected’, etc.

174. Once, as I was walking up and down in a good man’s shop, lamenting my sad and miserable state, afflicting myself with self-loathing for this wicked and ungodly thought, and grieving over my hard luck in committing so great a sin, I greatly feared that I would not be pardoned. I was also praying in my heart that if this sin of mine was different from the sin against the Holy Spirit, the Lord would show me. And as I was now ready to sink with fear, suddenly it was as if the noise of a wind had rushed in on me through the window, but very pleasant, and as if I heard a voice speaking: Did you ever refuse to be justified by the blood of Christ? At the same moment my whole past life and profession were opened to me, and I was made to see that I had not done so on purpose. So my heart answered with a groan, No. Then this word of God fell on me with power: ‘See that ye refuse not him that speaketh’ (Heb. 12:25). This took a strange hold on my spirit. It brought light with it, and commanded silence in my heart to all those riotous thoughts that used to roar and bellow and make a hideous noise within me like masterless hounds of hell. It also showed me that Jesus Christ still had a word of grace and mercy for me, and that He had not, as I had feared, completely forsaken and cast off my soul. Indeed, it was a kind of rebuke for my tendency to despair, a kind of warning to me if I did not, in spite of my sins and their terrible nature, risk my salvation on the Son of God. But as for deciding about this strange experience, I did not know what it was or where it came from. Even in twenty years I have not yet been able to form a judgment about it. What I thought then, I would be reluctant to say here. But truly, that sudden rushing wind was as if an angel had come upon me. But I will leave both it and the salvation until the day of judgment. I will only say this: it commanded a great calm in my soul; it persuaded me that there might be hope; it showed me, as I thought, what the unpardonable sin was, and that my soul still had the blessed privilege of fleeing to Jesus for mercy. But, I say, I still do not know what to say about this experience. That was in fact the reason I did not speak of it in the book at first. I now leave it for people of sound judgment to think about. I do not rest the weight of my salvation on it, but on the Lord Jesus in the promise. Yet since I am laying out my secret things here, I thought it might not be altogether unfitting to let this be shown too, though I cannot now describe it as I experienced it then. Its sweetness lasted for about three or four days, and then I began to doubt and despair again.

175. So my life still hung in doubt before me, not knowing which way I would tip. I only found that my soul wanted to throw itself at the feet of grace by prayer and pleading. But oh, it was hard for me now to find the face to pray for mercy to this Christ against whom I had sinned so vilely. It was hard work, I say, to try to look Him in the face against whom I had sinned so vilely. Indeed, I have found it as hard to come to God in prayer after backsliding from Him as to do anything else. Oh, the shame that went with me now, especially when I thought, I am now going to pray for mercy to Him whom I valued so lightly only a little while ago! I was ashamed, indeed utterly confounded, because I had committed this villainy. But I saw that there was only one way for me. I must go to Him and humble myself before Him, and beg that in His wonderful mercy He would show pity to me and have mercy on my wretched sinful soul.

176. When the tempter saw this, he strongly suggested to me that I ought not to pray to God, for prayer was not for anyone in my situation, nor could it do me any good, because I had rejected the Mediator through whom all prayer comes acceptably to God the Father, and without whom no prayer can come into His presence. So now to pray is only to add sin to sin. Indeed, to pray now, when God has cast you off, is the surest way to anger and offend Him more than you ever have before.

177. For God, he said, has been tired of you for several years already, because you are not one of His. Your bawling in His ears has been no pleasant sound to Him. That is why He let you commit this sin, so that you might be cut off completely. And will you still pray? The devil pressed this, and set before me the passage in Numbers where Moses told the children of Israel that because they would not go up to possess the land when God wanted them to, God shut them out of it for ever after, though they prayed with tears that they might go (Num. 14:36-37, etc.).

178. As it says in another place (Exod. 21:14), the man who sins presumptuously shall be taken from God’s altar so that he may die, just as Joab was taken by King Solomon when he thought he would find shelter there (1 Kings 2:28, etc.). These passages pinched me very painfully. Yet since my case was desperate, I thought to myself, I can only die. And if it must be so, at least it will be said that such a one died at the feet of Christ in prayer. This I did, but with great difficulty, God knows. For along with it, that saying about Esau would still be set at my heart like a flaming sword, to guard the way to the tree of life, in case I should taste of it and live. Oh, who knows how hard I found it to come to God in prayer?

179. I also wanted the prayers of God’s people for me, but I feared that God would give them no heart to do it. Indeed, I trembled in my soul to think that one or other of them would soon tell me that God had said to them the words He once said to the prophet about the children of Israel, ‘Pray thou not for this people,’ for I have rejected them (Jer. 11:14); so, Do not pray for him, for I have rejected him. Indeed, I thought He had whispered this to some of them already, only they dared not tell me so. Nor did I dare ask them about it, for fear that if it was so, it would drive me completely out of my mind. Man knows the beginning of sin, said Spira, but who sets the limits of where it ends?

180. About this time I took an opportunity to open my mind to an old Christian and told him my whole case. I also told him I was afraid I had committed the sin against the Holy Spirit, and he told me he thought so too. So here I got only cold comfort. But talking with him a little more, I found that, though he was a good man, he was a stranger to much fighting with the devil. So I went back to God again, as well as I could, still seeking mercy.

181. Now the tempter also began to mock me in my misery. He said that since I had parted with the Lord Jesus in this way and provoked to anger the One who would have stood between my soul and the flame of devouring fire, there was now only one way left: to pray that God the Father would be the Mediator between His Son and me, so that we might be reconciled again and I might have the blessed benefit in Him that His blessed saints enjoyed.

182. Then this Scripture seized my soul: He is of one mind, and who can turn Him? Oh, I saw that it would be as easy to persuade Him to make a new world, a new covenant or a new Bible besides the one we already have, as to pray for such a thing. This would be to persuade Him that what He had already done was mere folly, and to plead with Him to change, indeed to cancel, the whole way of salvation. And then this saying would tear my soul apart: ‘Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven, given among men, whereby we must be saved’ (Acts 4:12).

183. Now the freest, fullest and most gracious words of the gospel were the greatest torment to me. Indeed, nothing afflicted me so much as thoughts of Jesus Christ, the memory of a Saviour, because I had cast Him off. It brought to mind the villainy of my sin and what I had lost by it. Nothing stung my conscience like this. Every time I thought of the Lord Jesus, of His grace, love, goodness, kindness, gentleness, meekness, death, blood, promises and blessed appeals, comforts and consolations, it went into my soul like a sword. For along with these thoughts of the Lord Jesus, these other thoughts would always make room for themselves in my heart: Yes, this is the Jesus, the loving Saviour, the Son of God, whom you have parted with, whom you belittled, despised and abused. This is the only Saviour, the only Redeemer, the only one who could love sinners so much as to wash them from their sins in His own most precious blood. But you have no part or share in this Jesus. You have put Him away from you; you have said in your heart, Let Him go if He will. So now you are cut off from Him; you have cut yourself off from Him. Look at His goodness, then, but you yourself will have no share in it. Oh, I thought, what have I lost! What have I parted with! What have I robbed my poor soul of! Oh, it is a sad thing to be destroyed by the grace and mercy of God, to have the Lamb, the Saviour, turn into a lion and a destroyer (Rev. 6). I also trembled, as I have said, at the sight of God’s saints, especially those who loved Him greatly and made it their business to walk with Him continually in this world. For by their words, their conduct and all their signs of tenderness and fear of sinning against their precious Saviour, they condemned me, laid guilt on me, and added constant affliction and shame to my soul. The dread of them was on me, and I trembled at God’s Samuels (1 Sam. 16:4).

184. Now the tempter also began to mock my soul afresh in another way. He said that Christ did indeed pity my case and was sorry for my loss, but because I had sinned and transgressed as I had, He could not possibly help me or save me from what I feared. For my sin was not of the same kind as the sins of those for whom He bled and died, and it was not counted among those laid to His charge when He hung on the tree. So unless He came down from heaven and died again for this sin, I could have no benefit from Him, even though He did greatly pity me. These things may seem ridiculous to others, as ridiculous as they were in themselves, but to me they were most tormenting thoughts. Every one of them increased my misery: that Jesus Christ should have so much love as to pity me when He could not help me. Nor did I think the reason He could not help me was that His merits were weak, or that His grace and salvation had already been used up on others. It was because His faithfulness to His warnings would not let Him extend His mercy to me. Besides, as I have already hinted, I thought that my sin was not within the bounds of the pardon wrapped up in a promise. And if it was not, then I knew for certain that it would be easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for me to have eternal life. So the root of all these fears of mine was a firm belief in the reliability of the holy Word of God, together with being misinformed about the nature of my sin.

185. But oh, how it added to my affliction to imagine that I was guilty of a sin for which He did not die! These thoughts would so confuse me, imprison me and tie me up from faith that I did not know what to do. But oh, I thought, if only He would come down again! Oh, if only the work of man’s redemption was still to be done by Christ! How I would pray to Him and beg Him to count and reckon this sin among the rest for which He died! But this Scripture would strike me down as if dead: ‘Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more; death hath no more dominion over him’ (Rom. 6:9).

186. So by the strange and unusual attacks of the tempter my soul was like a broken ship, driven by the winds and tossed sometimes headlong into despair, sometimes onto the covenant of works, and sometimes into wishing that the new covenant and its conditions might be turned another way and changed, as far as I thought they concerned me. But in all these I was only like those who crash against the rocks, more broken, scattered and torn. Oh, the unimagined fancies, frights, fears and terrors produced by a thorough application of guilt when it gives way to despair! This is the man who has ‘his dwelling among the tombs’ with the dead, always crying out and ‘cutting himself with stones’ (Mark 5:2-5). But, I say, it is all in vain. Despair will not comfort him; the old covenant will not save him. No, heaven and earth will pass away before one jot or tittle of the Word and law of grace fails or is removed. This I saw, this I felt, and under this I groaned. Yet I gained this advantage from it: a further confirmation of the certainty of the way of salvation, and that the Scriptures were the Word of God. Oh, I cannot now describe what I saw and felt then of the steadfastness of Jesus Christ, the rock of man’s salvation. What was done could not be undone, added to or altered. I saw indeed that sin might drive the soul beyond Christ, namely the sin that is unpardonable. But woe to the one who was driven like that, for the Word would shut him out.

187. So I was always sinking, whatever I thought or did. One day I walked to a neighbouring town, sat down on a bench in the street, and fell into very deep thought about the most fearful state my sin had brought me to. After brooding a long time I lifted up my head, but it seemed to me as if the sun shining in the sky begrudged me its light, and as if the very stones in the street and the tiles on the houses were set against me. It seemed to me that they all joined together to banish me out of the world. I was loathed by them and unfit to live among them or share in their benefits, because I had sinned against the Saviour. Oh, how much happier than me every creature was now! For they stood firm and kept their place, but I was gone and lost.

188. Then, bursting out in the bitterness of my soul, I said to myself with a grievous sigh, How can God comfort such a wretch as I am? No sooner had I said it than this came back to me, as an echo answers a voice: This sin is not unto death. At this it was as if I had been raised out of a grave, and I cried out again, Lord, how could You find such a word as this? For I was filled with wonder at how fitting and how unexpected the sentence was. The fitness of the word, the rightness of its timing, the power and sweetness and light and glory that came with it, were marvellous to me. For the time being I was now free from doubt about the very thing I had been so doubtful about before. My fears had been that my sin was not pardonable, and so that I had no right to pray, to repent and so on, or that if I did, it would be of no advantage or profit to me. But now, I thought, if this sin is not unto death, then it is pardonable. So from this I have encouragement to come to God through Christ for mercy, and to regard the promise of forgiveness as standing with open arms to receive me as well as others. This was a great relief to my mind: that my sin was pardonable, that it was not the sin unto death (1 John 5:16-17). No one but those who know from their own experience what my trouble was can tell what relief came to my soul from this thought. It was a release from my former chains and a shelter from my former storm. I now seemed to stand on the same ground as other sinners, and to have as good a right to the Word and to prayer as any of them.

189. Now, I say, I hoped that my sin was not unpardonable, but that there might be hope of my obtaining forgiveness. But oh, how Satan now laid about him to bring me down again! But he could not do it at all, neither that day nor most of the next, for this sentence stood like a mill-post at my back. Yet towards the evening of the next day I felt this word begin to leave me and withdraw its support from me, and so I went back to my old fears again, but with a great deal of grumbling and fretfulness, for I feared the sorrow of despair. Nor could my faith hold on to this word any longer.

190. But the next day, in the evening, being under many fears, I went to seek the Lord. As I prayed, I cried, and my soul cried to Him with strong cries in these words: O Lord, I beg You, show me that You have loved me with an everlasting love (Jer. 31:3). No sooner had I said it than this came back to me sweetly, like an echo or a sounding again: ‘I have loved thee with an everlasting love.’ Now I went to bed in peace. And when I woke the next morning it was fresh on my soul, and I believed it.

191. But still the tempter did not leave me. That day he worked no fewer than a hundred times to break my peace. Oh, the battles and conflicts I met with then as I struggled to hold on to this word! That saying about Esau would fly in my face like lightning. I would sometimes go up and down twenty times in an hour. Yet God held me up and kept my heart on this word, from which I also had a great deal of sweetness and comforting hope of pardon for several days together. For this is how it was explained to me: I loved you while you were committing this sin; I loved you before; I love you still; and I will love you for ever.

192. Yet I saw my sin as most barbarous and a filthy crime, and I could not help concluding, with great shame and astonishment, that I had horribly abused the holy Son of God. So I felt my soul greatly love and pity Him, and my inmost being yearn towards Him, for I saw that He was still my Friend and was repaying me good for evil. Indeed, the love and affection that then burned within me for my Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ produced at this time such a strong and hot desire for revenge on myself for the wrong I had done Him that, to speak as I thought then, if I had had a thousand gallons of blood in my veins, I could freely have spilt it all at the command and feet of my Lord and Saviour.

193. And as I was thinking and studying like this, considering how to love the Lord and express my love to Him, this saying came in on me: ‘If thou, Lord, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand? But there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared’ (Ps. 130:3-4). These were good words to me, especially the second part: that there is forgiveness with the Lord, so that He may be feared, that is, as I understood it then, so that He may be loved and reverenced. For it was explained to me like this: that the great God valued the love of His poor creatures so highly that rather than go without their love, He would pardon their sins.

194. And now this word was fulfilled in me, and I was also refreshed by it: Then shall they be ashamed and confounded, ‘and never open their mouth any more because of their shame, when I am pacified towards them for all that they have done, saith the Lord God’ (Ezek. 16:63). So at this time my soul was set free, and as I thought then, for ever, from being afflicted again with my former guilt and bewilderment.

195. But before many weeks were over I began to lose heart again, fearing that in spite of all I had enjoyed I might still be deceived and destroyed in the end. For this thought came strongly into my mind: that whatever comfort and peace I thought I might have from the word of the promise of life, unless the Scriptures could be found to agree with and support my refreshment, then whatever I might think of it, and however tightly I held it, I would find no such thing at the end; ‘for the Scripture cannot be broken’ (John 10:35).

196. Now my heart began to ache again, and I feared I might meet with disappointment in the end. So I began very seriously to examine my former comfort, and to consider whether someone who had sinned as I had might confidently trust in the faithfulness of God set out in those words by which I had been comforted and on which I had leaned. But now these sayings were brought to my mind: ‘For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost, and have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come, if they shall fall away, to renew them again unto repentance’ (Heb. 6:4-6). ‘For if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins, but a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation, which shall devour the adversaries’ (Heb. 10:26-27). Even ‘as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright; for ye know how that afterward, when he would have inherited the blessing, he was rejected; for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears’ (Heb. 12:16-17).

197. Now the word of the gospel was forced out of my soul, so that no promise or encouragement was to be found in the Bible for me. And now this saying would work on my spirit to afflict me: ‘Rejoice not, O Israel, for joy as other people’ (Hos. 9:1). For I saw that there was indeed cause for rejoicing for those who held on to Jesus. But as for me, I had cut myself off by my sins, and had left myself neither a foothold nor a handhold among all the supports and props in the precious word of life.

198. And truly I now felt myself sinking into a gulf, like a house whose foundation has been destroyed. In this condition I compared myself to a child who has fallen into a mill-pond. Though it can manage to scrabble and thrash about in the water, it can find no hold for hand or foot, and so in the end it must die in that condition. As soon as this fresh attack had fastened on my soul, this Scripture came into my heart: ‘This is for many days’ (Dan. 10:14). And indeed I found that it was so, for I could not be delivered or brought to peace again until nearly two and a half years had fully passed. So these words, though in themselves they tended to discourage, were at times a help and refreshment to me, since I feared this condition would be eternal.

199. For, I thought, many days are not for ever; many days will come to an end. So since I was to be afflicted not for a few days but for many, I was glad it was only for many days. In this way, I say, I could sometimes pull myself together and give myself some help. For as soon as the words first came into my mind, I knew my trouble would be long. Yet this was only sometimes, for I could not always think about it, nor was I always helped by it when I did.

200. While these Scriptures lay before me and laid sin afresh at my door, the saying in the eighteenth chapter of Luke, along with others, encouraged me to pray. Then the tempter attacked me again very fiercely, suggesting that neither the mercy of God nor the blood of Christ concerned me at all, nor could they help me with my sin, so it was useless to pray. Yet, I thought, I will pray. But, said the tempter, your sin is unpardonable. Well, I said, I will pray. It is no use, he said. Yet, I said, I will pray. So I went to prayer to God, and while I was praying I said words to this effect: Lord, Satan tells me that neither Your mercy nor Christ’s blood is enough to save my soul. Lord, will I honour You most by believing that You will and can, or him by believing that You neither will nor can? Lord, I would gladly honour You by believing that You will and can.

201. And as I was before the Lord like this, this Scripture fastened on my heart: ‘O man, great is thy faith’ (Matt. 15:28), just as if someone had clapped me on the back as I knelt before God. Yet I was not able to believe that this was a prayer of faith until almost six months later. For I could not think that I had faith, or that there was any word for me to put my faith in. So I was still stuck, as it were, in the jaws of despair, and went about mourning in a sad condition, crying, Is His mercy completely gone? Is His mercy completely gone for ever? And sometimes I thought, even while I was groaning out these words, that they seemed to make it a question whether it was or not. Yet I greatly feared that it was.

202. There was nothing I longed for more now than to be put out of doubt about this question. And as I was intensely longing to know whether there was really hope for me, these words came rolling into my mind: ‘Will the Lord cast off for ever? and will he be favourable no more? Is his mercy clean gone for ever? Doth his promise fail for evermore? Hath God forgotten to be gracious? Hath he in anger shut up his tender mercies?’ (Ps. 77:7-9). All the while they ran through my mind, it seemed to me that I still had this as the answer: It is a question whether He has or not; perhaps He has not. Indeed, the question seemed to me to carry within it a sure assurance that He had not cast off and would not, but would be favourable; that His promise does not fail; and that He had not forgotten to be gracious, nor would in anger shut up His tender mercy. At the same time there was also something else on my heart which I cannot now call to mind. Together with this text, it sweetened my heart and made me conclude that His mercy might not be entirely gone, nor completely gone for ever.

203. Another time, I remember, I was again deeply troubled by the question whether the blood of Christ was enough to save my soul. I stayed in this doubt from morning until about seven or eight at night. At last, when I was quite worn out, as it were, with fear that it would not take hold of me, these words sounded suddenly in my heart: He is able. It seemed to me that this word able was spoken so loudly to me. It appeared such a great word; it seemed to be written in great letters, and it gave my fear and doubt such a jolt, for the time it stayed with me, which was about a day, as I never had in all my life before or since (Heb. 7:25).

204. But one morning, when I was praying again and trembling under the fear that no word of God could help me, this piece of a sentence darted in on me: ‘My grace is sufficient.’ At this I seemed to feel some support, as if there might be hope. But oh, what a good thing it is for God to send His word! For about two weeks before, I had been looking at this very place, and then I thought it could not come near my soul with comfort, so I threw down my book in a huff. Then I thought it was not big enough for me, no, not big enough. But now it was as if it had arms of grace so wide that it could enfold not only me but many more besides.

205. I was held up by these words, though not without intense conflicts, for about seven or eight weeks. For my peace would come and go, sometimes twenty times a day: comfort now and trouble soon after; peace now, and before I could walk a furlong, as full of fear and guilt as any heart could hold. And this was not just now and then, but my whole seven weeks’ experience. For this word about the sufficiency of grace, and that one about Esau parting with his birthright, were like a pair of scales in my mind. Sometimes one end would be uppermost, and sometimes the other, and my peace or trouble went accordingly.

206. So I kept praying to God that He would bring this Scripture home more fully to my heart, that is, that He would help me to apply the whole sentence, for as yet I could not. What He gave, I gathered, but I could go no further. As yet it only helped me to hope that there might be mercy for me: ‘My grace is sufficient’. And though it came no further, it answered my earlier question, that there was hope. Yet because ‘for thee’ was left out, I was not content, but prayed to God for that too. So one day, as I was in a meeting of God’s people, full of sadness and terror, for my fears were strong on me again, and I was thinking that my soul was no better but my case most sad and fearful, these words suddenly broke in on me with great power: ‘My grace is sufficient for thee, my grace is sufficient for thee, my grace is sufficient for thee,’ three times over. And oh, it seemed to me that every word was a mighty word to me, my, and grace, and sufficient, and for thee. They were then, and sometimes still are, far bigger than other words.

207. At that time my understanding was so enlightened that it was as though I had seen the Lord Jesus look down from heaven through the roof tiles at me and direct these words to me. This sent me home mourning. It broke my heart, filled me with joy and laid me as low as the dust. It did not stay with me long, I mean in this glory and refreshing comfort, yet it remained with me for several weeks and encouraged me to hope. But as soon as its powerful working was taken from my heart, that other word about Esau came back on me as before. So my soul hung again as if in a pair of scales, sometimes up and sometimes down, now in peace and soon again in terror.

208. I went on like this for many weeks, sometimes comforted and sometimes tormented. At certain times especially my torment would be very severe, for all those Scriptures in Hebrews mentioned earlier would be set before me as the only sentences that would keep me out of heaven. Then again I would begin to regret that the thought had ever gone through me. I would also think to myself, Why, how many Scriptures are there against me? There are only three or four. Can God not pass them by and save me in spite of them all? At other times I would think, Oh, if it were not for these three or four words, how I might be comforted now! And at times I could hardly help wishing them out of the book.

209. Then it seemed to me as if Peter and Paul and John and all the writers looked on me with scorn and held me in derision, and as if they said to me, All our words are truth, one as forceful as another. It is not we who have cut you off; you have thrown yourself away. There are none of our sentences that you must take hold of but these and ones like them: ‘It is impossible; there remains no more sacrifice for sin’ (Heb. 6). And ‘it had been better for them not to have known’ the will of God, ‘than, after they have known it, to turn from the holy commandment delivered unto them’ (2 Pet. 2:21). ‘For the Scriptures cannot be broken.’

210. I saw that these, like the elders of the city of refuge, were to be the judges both of my case and of me, while I stood with the avenger of blood at my heels, trembling at their gate for deliverance. With a thousand fears and suspicions, I doubted that they would shut me out for ever (Josh. 20:3-4).

211. So I was bewildered, not knowing what to do or how to be satisfied on this question: Could the Scriptures agree in the salvation of my soul? I trembled at the apostles. I knew their words were true and that they must stand for ever.

212. I remember one day, as I was going through different states of mind, and noticing that these states always matched the nature of whatever Scripture came into my mind (if this one about grace, I was quiet; but if that one about Esau, then I was tormented), I thought, Lord, if both these Scriptures would meet in my heart at once, I wonder which of them would get the better of me. So it seemed to me that I longed for them both to come on me together. Indeed, I asked God that they might.

213. Well, about two or three days later they did indeed. They both burst in on me at once, and worked and struggled strangely in me for a while. At last the one about Esau’s birthright began to grow weak and draw back and vanish, and this one about the sufficiency of grace won out, with peace and joy. And as I was pondering this, this Scripture came home to me: ‘Mercy rejoiceth against judgment’ (Jas. 2:13).

214. This was a wonder to me. Yet truly I am inclined to think it was from God. For the word of the law and of wrath must give way to the word of life and grace, because although the word of condemnation is glorious, the word of life and salvation far surpasses it in glory (2 Cor. 3:8-12; Mark 9:5-7). It also shows that Moses and Elijah must both vanish and leave Christ and His saints alone.

215. This Scripture also visited my soul most sweetly: ‘And him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out’ (John 6:37). Oh, the comfort I have had from these words, ‘in no wise’! It is as if He were saying, by no means, for nothing at all, whatever he has done. But Satan would work hard to pull this promise away from me, telling me that Christ did not mean me and people like me, but sinners of a lower rank who had not done what I had done. But I would answer him back, Satan, there is no such exception in this word, but ‘him that comes’, him, any him: ‘him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.’ And I still remember this well: of all the tricks Satan used to take this Scripture from me, he never once put this question, But are you coming the right way? I have thought the reason was that he thought I knew very well what coming the right way was. For I saw that to come the right way was to come as I was, a vile and ungodly sinner, and to throw myself at the feet of mercy, condemning myself for sin. If ever Satan and I fought over any word of God in all my life, it was over this good word of Christ, he at one end and I at the other. Oh, what a struggle we had! It was over this verse in John, I say, that we tugged and strove so. He pulled and I pulled, but God be praised, I got the better of him; I got some sweetness from it.

216. But in spite of all these helps and blessed words of grace, that word about Esau selling his birthright would still trouble my conscience at times. For though I had been comforted most sweetly, and only just before, when that came into my mind it would make me afraid again. I could not be completely rid of it; it would be with me every day. So now I set about it another way, by considering the nature of this blasphemous thought, I mean if I took the words in their widest sense and gave every word in it its own natural force and scope. When I had considered it like this, I found that, taken fairly, they came to this: that I had freely left the Lord Jesus Christ to choose whether He would be my Saviour or not. For the wicked words were these: Let Him go if He will. Then this Scripture gave me hope: ‘I will never leave thee nor forsake thee’ (Heb. 13:5). O Lord, I said, but I have left You. Then it answered again, ‘But I will not leave thee.’ For this too I thank God.

217. Yet I was terribly afraid that He would, and I found it extremely hard to trust Him, seeing that I had offended Him so much. I would have been very glad if this thought had never happened to me, for then I thought I could have leaned on His grace much more easily and freely. I see that it was with me as it was with Joseph’s brothers: the guilt of their own wickedness often filled them with fear that their brother would despise them in the end (Gen. 50:15-17).

218. But of all the Scriptures I had yet come across, the one in the twentieth chapter of Joshua was the greatest comfort to me. It speaks of the slayer who was to flee for refuge. And if the avenger of blood pursues the slayer, then, says Moses, the elders of the city of refuge shall not hand him over, because he struck his neighbour unintentionally and did not hate him beforehand. Oh, blessed be God for this word! I was convinced that I was the slayer, and I felt with great terror that the avenger of blood was pursuing me. All that remained now was to ask whether I had the right to enter the city of refuge. I found that the one who lay in wait to shed blood must not enter. It was not the deliberate murderer, but the one who did it unintentionally, who shed blood unawares, not out of spite or grudge or malice; the one who shed it unintentionally, who had not hated his neighbour before. Therefore:

219. I truly thought I was the man who must enter, because I had struck my neighbour unintentionally and had not hated him beforehand. I had not hated Him beforehand. No, I had prayed to Him and been careful not to sin against Him. Indeed, I had struggled against this wicked temptation for a year before. And even when it passed through my heart, it did so in spite of everything I could do. So I thought I had the right to enter this city, and the elders, who are the apostles, were not to hand me over. This was a great comfort to me and gave me much ground for hope.

220. Yet I was very exacting, for my pain had brought me to the point where I did not know what ground was firm enough to hold me. There was one question my soul greatly wanted settled: Is it possible for any soul that has truly committed the unpardonable sin to receive afterwards even the smallest true spiritual comfort from God through Christ? After thinking about it a great deal, I found that the answer was no, they could not, and for these reasons:

221. First, because those who have committed that sin are barred from any share in the blood of Christ. Being shut out of that, they must be without the least ground of hope, and so of spiritual comfort, for to such people ‘there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins’ (Heb. 10:26). Second, because they are denied any share in the promise of life. They will never be forgiven, ‘neither in this world, neither in that which is to come’ (Matt. 12:32). Third, the Son of God also shuts them out from any share in His blessed intercession, being for ever ashamed to own them before His holy Father and the blessed angels in heaven (Mark 8:38).

222. When I had considered this matter with much thought, and could not help concluding that the Lord had comforted me, and that after this wicked sin of mine, it seemed to me that I could dare to come near those most fearful and terrible Scriptures that had frightened me so much all this while. Before, I had hardly dared to glance at them. Indeed, a hundred times I could barely stop myself wishing them out of the Bible, for I thought they would destroy me. But now, I say, I began to take some measure of courage to come close to them, to read them and consider them, and to weigh their scope and purpose.

223. When I began to do this, I found their face had changed, for they did not look as grimly at me as I had thought before. First I came to the sixth chapter of Hebrews, still trembling for fear it would strike me. When I had considered it, I found that the falling it refers to is a falling away completely, that is, as I understood it, a falling from and an outright denial of the gospel of the forgiveness of sins through Christ, for the apostle begins his argument from these things (verses 1-3). Second, I found that this falling away must be done openly, in full view of the world, so as ‘to put Christ to an open shame’. Third, I found that the people it refers to are shut up by God for ever in blindness, hardness and impenitence: it is impossible for them to be renewed again to repentance. By all these particulars I found, to God’s everlasting praise, that my sin was not the sin meant in this place.

First, I admitted that I had fallen, but not fallen away, that is, from the profession of faith in Jesus to eternal life. Second, I admitted that I had put Jesus Christ to shame by my sin, but not to open shame. I did not deny Him before people, or condemn Him as worthless before the world. Third, nor did I find that God had shut me up or refused to let me come, though I did indeed find it hard work to come to Him in sorrow and repentance. Blessed be God for unsearchable grace.

224. Then I considered the passage in the tenth chapter of Hebrews, and found that the wilful sin mentioned there is not every wilful sin, but the one that throws off Christ and then His commandments too. Second, it must also be done openly, before two or three witnesses, to correspond with the law (verse 28). Third, this sin cannot be committed without doing great insult to the Spirit of grace, despising both the warnings against that sin and the appeals to do the opposite. But the Lord knows that, devilish as this sin of mine was, it did not amount to these.

225. And as for the passage in the twelfth chapter of Hebrews about Esau selling his birthright, though this was the one that killed me and stood like a spear against me, I now considered these things. First, his was not a hasty thought against the constant struggle of his mind, but a thought he consented to and also put into practice, and that after some deliberation (Gen. 25). Second, it was a public and open action, before his brother at least, if not before many more. This made his sin far more serious than it would otherwise have been. Third, he went on despising his birthright: ‘He did eat and drink, and went his way; thus Esau despised his birthright’ (verse 34). Indeed, twenty years later he was found to despise it still: ‘And Esau said, I have enough, my brother; keep that thou hast unto thyself’ (Gen. 33:9).

226. Now as for Esau seeking a place of repentance, this is what I thought. First, this was not for the birthright but for the blessing. This is clear from the apostle, and Esau himself makes the distinction: ‘He took away my birthright (that is, before); and behold, now he hath taken away my blessing’ (Gen. 27:36). Second, having considered this, I came back to the apostle to see what God’s mind might be about Esau’s sin in a New Testament manner and sense. As far as I could understand it, God’s meaning was this: that the birthright stood for regeneration, and the blessing for the eternal inheritance. For the apostle seems to hint at this: ‘Lest there be any profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright’. It is as if he were saying, In case there is anyone among you who throws off all those blessed beginnings God is now working in him towards a new birth, in case they become like Esau and are rejected afterwards when they want to inherit the blessing.

227. For there are many who, in the day of grace and mercy, despise the very things that are the birthright to heaven, and who yet, when the day of decision comes, will cry as loudly as Esau, ‘Lord, Lord, open to us’. But then, just as Isaac would not change his mind, neither will God the Father. He will say, I have blessed these, and they shall be blessed; but as for you, depart from me, all you workers of iniquity (Gen. 27:33; Luke 13:25-27).

228. When I had considered these Scriptures in this way, and found that understanding them like this was not against other Scriptures but in line with them, it added still more to my encouragement and comfort. It also dealt a great blow to that objection, that the Scriptures could not agree in the salvation of my soul. And now there remained only the tail end of the storm, for the thunder had gone past me. Only some drops still remained that would fall on me now and then. But because my earlier frights and anguish had been so severe and deep, it often still happened to me as it happens to those who have been frightened by fire: I thought every voice was crying Fire, fire. Every little touch would hurt my tender conscience.

229. But one day, as I was crossing a field, and that with some jolts to my conscience, fearing that all was still not right, suddenly this sentence fell on my soul: Your righteousness is in heaven. And with it, it seemed to me that I saw with the eyes of my soul Jesus Christ at God’s right hand. There, I say, is my righteousness. So wherever I was, or whatever I was doing, God could not say of me, He lacks my righteousness, for that was right in front of Him. I also saw, moreover, that it was not my good frame of heart that made my righteousness better, nor my bad frame that made it worse. For my righteousness was Jesus Christ Himself, the same yesterday, and today, and for ever (Heb. 13:8).

230. Now my chains really fell off my legs. I was set free from my affliction and irons; my temptations had fled away. So from that time on those dreadful Scriptures of God stopped troubling me. Now I also went home rejoicing in the grace and love of God. When I got home, I looked to see if I could find that sentence, Your righteousness is in heaven, but I could not find such a saying. So my heart began to sink again. Only this was brought to my memory: He ‘of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption’. By this word I saw that the other sentence was true (1 Cor. 1:30).

231. For by this Scripture I saw that the man Christ Jesus, as He is distinct from us in His bodily presence, is our righteousness and sanctification before God. So I lived here for some time, very sweetly at peace with God through Christ. Oh, I thought, Christ! Christ! There was nothing but Christ before my eyes. I was not just looking at this and that benefit of Christ separately, such as His blood, burial or resurrection, but considered Him as a whole Christ, as the One in whom all these and all His other virtues, relationships, offices and works met together, and that as He sat at the right hand of God in heaven.

232. It was glorious to me to see His exaltation, and the worth and power of all His benefits, and this was why: now I could look away from myself to Him, and reckon that all those graces of God that were now green in me were only like the cracked small coins that rich men carry in their purses while their gold is in their chests at home! Oh, I saw that my gold was in my chest at home, in Christ, my Lord and Saviour! Now Christ was all: all my wisdom, all my righteousness, all my sanctification and all my redemption.

233. Further, the Lord also led me into the mystery of union with the Son of God: that I was joined to Him, that I was flesh of His flesh and bone of His bone. Now that word in Ephesians 5:30 was sweet to me. By this too my faith in Him as my righteousness was confirmed all the more. For if He and I were one, then His righteousness was mine, His merits were mine, His victory was mine too. Now I could see myself in heaven and on earth at once: in heaven by my Christ, by my head, by my righteousness and life, though on earth by my body or person.

234. Now I saw that Christ Jesus was regarded by God, and should also be regarded by us, as that common or public person in whom the whole body of His elect is always to be considered and counted. We fulfilled the law through Him, rose from the dead through Him, and won the victory over sin, death, the devil and hell through Him. When He died, we died, and the same with His resurrection. ‘Thy dead men shall live, together with my dead body shall they arise,’ He says (Isa. 26:19).
