And again, ‘After two days will he revive us: in the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight’ (Hos. 6:2). This is now fulfilled by the Son of Man sitting down at the right hand of the Majesty in the heavens, according to the words to the Ephesians: He ‘hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus’ (Eph. 2:6).

235. Ah, these blessed thoughts and Scriptures, with many others like them, were made to sparkle in my eyes in those days, so that I have reason to say, ‘Praise ye the Lord. Praise God in his sanctuary: praise him in the firmament of his power. Praise him for his mighty acts: praise him according to his excellent greatness’ (Ps. 150:1-2).

236. I have now given you, in a few words, a taste of the sorrow and affliction my soul went through because of the guilt and terror this wicked thought of mine laid on me. I have also given you a glimpse of my deliverance from it, and of the sweet and blessed comfort I met with afterwards, which comfort stayed in my heart for about a year, to my unspeakable wonder. So now, God willing, before I go any further, I will tell you in a word or two what I understand to have been the cause of this temptation, and after that, what benefit it became to my soul in the end.

237. As for the causes, I understood them to be chiefly two, and I was deeply convinced of both of them all the time this trouble lay on me. The first was that when I was delivered from the temptation that came before, I did not go on praying to God to keep me from temptations still to come. For though, as I can truthfully say, my soul was much in prayer before this trial seized me, I prayed only, or at least mainly, for the removal of present troubles and for fresh discoveries of His love in Christ. I saw afterwards that this was not enough. I should also have prayed that the great God would keep me from the evil to come.

238. I was made deeply aware of this by the prayer of holy David, who, while he was enjoying present mercy, still prayed that God would hold him back from sin and temptation to come. ‘Then,’ he says, ‘shall I be upright, I shall be innocent from the great transgression’ (Ps. 19:13). By this very word I was stung and condemned all the way through this long temptation.

239. Another word that strongly condemned my folly in neglecting this duty was this (Heb. 4:16): ‘Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.’ I had not done this, and so I was allowed to sin and fall like this, as it is written, ‘Pray that ye enter not into temptation.’ And truly this very thing still weighs on me with such awe to this day that when I come before the Lord I dare not get up off my knees until I have asked Him for help and mercy against the temptations to come. And I beg you, reader, to learn to beware of my carelessness, from the affliction I suffered with sorrow for this for days and months and years.

240. Another cause of this temptation was that I had tempted God, and this is how I did it. At one time my wife was pregnant, and before her time was up, pains like those of a woman in labour came on her fiercely and strongly, as if she would go into labour at once and give birth too early. It was at this very time that I had been so strongly tempted to question the existence of God. So as my wife lay crying beside me, I said, but in the greatest secrecy imaginable, only thinking it in my heart, Lord, if You will now remove this sad affliction from my wife, and make her troubled with it no more tonight (and now her pains were just upon her), then I will know that You can discern the most secret thoughts of the heart.

241. No sooner had I said it in my heart than her pains were taken away, and she fell into a deep sleep and stayed like that until morning. At this I was greatly amazed, not knowing what to think. But after I had been awake a good while and heard her cry no more, I fell asleep too. When I woke in the morning, it came back to me what I had said in my heart the night before, and how the Lord had shown me that He knew my secret thoughts. This was a great astonishment to me for several weeks afterwards.

242. Well, about a year and a half later, that wicked, sinful thought I have spoken of went through my wicked heart, this very thought: Let Christ go if He will. So when I had fallen under guilt for this, the memory of my other thought and what came of it would also come on me with this retort, which carried a rebuke along with it: Now you can see that God does know the most secret thoughts of the heart.

243. And with this, the story of what passed between the Lord and His servant Gideon fell on my spirit. Because Gideon tested God with his fleece, both wet and dry, when he should have believed and taken Him at His word, the Lord afterwards tested him by sending him against a countless army of enemies, and that, to outward appearances, without any strength or help (Judg. 6-7). He dealt with me in the same way, and justly, for I should have believed His word and not put an if on the all-seeing knowledge of God.

244. And now to show you something of the benefits I also gained from this temptation. First, through it I was made to have constantly in my soul a very wonderful sense of both the existence and the glory of God and of His beloved Son. In the temptation before this, my soul was perplexed with unbelief, blasphemy, hardness of heart, and questions about the existence of God and Christ, the truth of the Word and the certainty of the world to come. Then, I say, I was greatly attacked and tormented with atheism. But now it was different. Now God and Christ were constantly before my face, though not in a comforting way, but with extreme dread and terror. At this time the glory of God’s holiness broke me to pieces, and the tender compassion of Christ broke me as on the wheel. For I could only think of Him as a lost and rejected Christ, and the memory of this was like the constant breaking of my bones.

245. Now the Scriptures also were wonderful things to me. I saw that their truth and reliability were the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Those whom the Scriptures favour must inherit bliss, but those whom they oppose and condemn must perish for evermore. Oh, this word, ‘For the Scriptures cannot be broken,’ would tear open the lining of my heart, and so would that other one, ‘Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained.’ Now I saw that the apostles were the elders of the city of refuge (Josh. 20:4). Those they were to take in were received to life, but those they shut out were to be killed by the avenger of blood.

246. Oh, one sentence of Scripture, I mean those sentences that stood against me, as I sometimes thought every one of them did, afflicted and terrified my mind more, I say, than an army of forty thousand men coming against me could have done. Woe to the one against whom the Scriptures set themselves.

247. Through this temptation I was made to see more into the nature of the promises than I ever had before. For as I now lay trembling under the mighty hand of God, constantly torn and broken by the thunderings of His justice, this made me turn over every page with an anxious heart and a watchful eye, with great seriousness, and with much diligence mixed with trembling consider every sentence, together with its natural force and breadth.

248. Through this temptation I was also thoroughly cured of my former foolish habit of brushing aside the word of promise when it came into my mind. For now, though I could not draw comfort and sweetness from the promise as I had at other times, I would grab at everything I saw, like a drowning man. Before, I thought I should not touch the promise unless I felt its comfort. But now was no time for that; the avenger of blood was pursuing me too hard.

249. So now I was glad to grab at that word, even though I feared I had no ground or right to claim it, and even to leap into the arms of that promise, though I feared it had shut its heart against me. Now too I would try hard to take the Word as God had set it down, without restricting the natural force of a single syllable of it. Oh, what I now saw in that blessed sixth chapter of John: ‘And him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out’ (verse 37). Now I began to think to myself that God had a bigger mouth to speak with than I had a heart to take it in. I also thought to myself that He did not speak His words in haste or in thoughtless heat, but with infinite wisdom and judgment, in real truth and faithfulness.

250. In those days, often in my greatest agonies, I would flounder towards the promise, as horses still stuck in the mud flounder towards firm ground, concluding, though like someone almost out of his mind with fear, On this I will rest and stay, and leave the fulfilling of it to the God of heaven who made it. Oh, many a tug-of-war my heart has had with Satan over that sixth chapter of John! I was not looking mainly for comfort now, as at other times, though oh, how welcome it would have been to me! But now a word, a word to lean a weary soul on, so that I might not sink for ever, was what I hunted for.

251. Indeed, often when I have been making for the promise, it has seemed to me as if the Lord would refuse my soul for ever. It was often as if I had run onto the pikes, and as if the Lord had thrust at me with a flaming sword to keep me from Him. Then I would think of Esther, who went to petition the king against the law (Esth. 4:16). I also thought of Benhadad’s servants, who went to their enemies with ropes on their heads to beg for mercy (1 Kings 20:31). The woman of Canaan too, who would not be put off though Christ called her a dog (Matt. 15:21-28), and the man who went to borrow bread at midnight (Luke 11:5-8), were great encouragements to me.

252. I never saw such heights and depths in grace and love and mercy as I saw after this temptation. Great sins draw out great grace. And where guilt is most terrible and fierce, there the mercy of God in Christ, when shown to the soul, appears most high and mighty. When Job had come through his captivity, he had ‘twice as much as he had before’ (Job 42:10). Blessed be God for Jesus Christ our Lord. There are many other things I could note here, but I want to be brief, so I will leave them out for now. I pray God that my hurts may make others afraid to offend, in case they too are made to bear the iron yoke as I did.

Two or three times, at or around the time of my deliverance from this temptation, I had such a strange sense of the grace of God that I could hardly bear up under it. It was so beyond measure amazing, when I thought it could reach me, that I really think if that sense of it had stayed on me long, it would have made me unfit for work.

253. Now I will go on to tell you about other ways the Lord led me, His dealings with me at various other times, and the temptations I met with then. I will begin with what I met when I first joined in fellowship with God’s people in Bedford. After I had told the church that I wished to walk with them in the order and ordinances of Christ, and had been admitted by them, as I thought about that blessed ordinance of Christ, His last supper with His disciples before His death, this Scripture, ‘This do in remembrance of me’ (Luke 22:19), was made a very precious word to me. For by it the Lord came down on my conscience, showing me His death for my sins, and, as I felt then, it was as if He plunged me into its power. But, look, I had not been taking part in that ordinance for long before such fierce and sad temptations came on me every time I was at it, both to blaspheme the ordinance and to wish some deadly thing on those who were eating it, that for fear I should at any time be guilty of consenting to these wicked and fearful thoughts, I was forced to strain myself the whole time in praying to God to keep me from such blasphemies, and also in crying to God to bless the bread and cup to them as they went from mouth to mouth. I have thought since that the reason for this temptation was that I did not at first come to take part in it with the reverence that was fitting for me.

254. I went on like this for nine months and could never find rest or ease. But at last the Lord came in on my soul with the same Scripture by which my soul had been visited before. Since then I have usually been very well and comforted in taking part in that blessed ordinance, and have, I trust, discerned in it the Lord’s body as broken for my sins, and that His precious blood has been shed for my transgressions.

255. At one time I was somewhat inclined to consumption, and around the spring I was suddenly and violently seized with great physical weakness, so much so that I thought I could not live. Now I began afresh to give myself to a serious examination of my state and condition for the future, and of my evidences for that blessed world to come. For it has been my usual practice, I bless the name of God, always and especially in the day of affliction, to try to keep my share in the life to come clear before my eyes.

256. But no sooner had I begun to call to mind my former experience of God’s goodness to my soul than a countless crowd of my sins and transgressions came flocking into my mind. Among these, the ones that troubled me most at this time were my deadness, dullness and coldness in holy duties, my wanderings of heart, my weariness in all good things, and my lack of love for God, His ways and His people. And at the end of it all came this: Are these the fruits of Christianity? Are these the marks of a blessed man?

257. When I grasped these things, my sickness was doubled, for now I was sick in my inner self. My soul was weighed down with guilt. Now too my former experience of God’s goodness to me was taken completely out of my mind and hidden as if it had never been or been seen. Now my soul was badly squeezed between these two thoughts: I must not live, and I dare not die. Now I sank and fell in my spirit and was giving everything up for lost. But as I was walking up and down in the house like a man in the most miserable state, this word of God took hold of my heart: Ye are ‘justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus’ (Rom. 3:24). But oh, what a turn it gave me!

258. Now I was like someone woken from a troubled sleep and dream. As I listened to this heavenly sentence, it was as if I heard it explained to me like this: Sinner, you think that because of your sins and weaknesses I cannot save your soul. But look, My Son is beside Me, and I look on Him, not on you, and will deal with you according to how pleased I am with Him. At this my mind was greatly lightened, and I was made to understand that God could justify a sinner at any time. It was only a matter of His looking on Christ and crediting His benefits to us, and the work was done at once.

259. And as I was pondering this, this Scripture also came with great power on my spirit: ‘Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us,’ etc. (Titus 3:5; 2 Tim. 1:9). Now I was lifted up high. I saw myself in the arms of grace and mercy. Though before I had been afraid to think of the hour of death, now I cried, Let me die. Now death was lovely and beautiful in my sight, for I saw that we will never truly live until we have gone to the other world. Oh, it seemed to me that this life is only a slumber compared with the life above. At this time too I saw more in the words ‘Heirs of God’ (Rom. 8:17) than I will ever be able to express while I live in this world. ‘Heirs of God’! God Himself is the portion of the saints. This I saw and wondered at, but I cannot tell you what I saw.

260. Again, at another time when I was very ill and weak, the tempter attacked me strongly the whole time. For I find that he is very keen to attack the soul when it begins to draw near the grave; that is his opportunity. He worked hard to hide my former experience of God’s goodness from me, and set before me the terrors of death and of God’s judgment. So at this time, through my fear of being lost for ever if I died now, I was like a dead man before death came, and it was as if I already felt myself going down into the pit. It seemed to me, I said, that there was no way but that I must go to hell. But look, just as I was in the middle of those fears, these words about the angels carrying Lazarus into Abraham’s bosom darted in on me, as if to say, So it will be with you when you leave this world. This sweetly revived my spirit and helped me to hope in God. When I had thought about it with comfort for a while, this word fell with great weight on my mind: ‘O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?’ (1 Cor. 15:55). At this I became well in both body and mind at once, for my sickness vanished immediately, and I went about my work for God in comfort again.

261. Another time, though just before I had been fairly well and lively in my spirit, a great cloud of darkness suddenly fell on me. It hid the things of God and Christ from me so completely that it was as if I had never seen or known them in my life. My soul was also so overrun by a senseless, heartless frame of spirit that I could not feel my soul move or stir after grace and life through Christ. It was as if my back had been broken, or as if my hands and feet had been tied or bound with chains. At this time I also felt some weakness seize my body, which made the other affliction all the heavier and more uncomfortable for me.

262. After I had been in this condition for some three or four days, as I was sitting by the fire, I suddenly felt this word sound in my heart: I must go to Jesus. At this my former darkness and atheism fled away, and the blessed things of heaven were set before my view. While I was overtaken with surprise like this so suddenly, I said, Wife, is there such a Scripture, I must go to Jesus? She said she could not tell. So I sat still thinking, to see if I could remember such a place. I had not sat more than two or three minutes before this came bursting in on me: ‘And to an innumerable company of angels,’ and along with it the twelfth chapter of Hebrews, about Mount Zion, was set before my eyes (verses 22-24).

263. Then with joy I told my wife, Oh, now I know, I know! That night was a good night for me; I have had few better. I longed for the company of some of God’s people, so that I might share with them what God had shown me. Christ was a precious Christ to my soul that night. I could hardly lie in my bed for joy and peace and triumph through Christ. This great glory did not stay with me until morning, yet that twelfth chapter of Hebrews (Heb. 12:22-24) was a blessed Scripture to me for many days together after this.

264. The words are these: ‘Ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels, to the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven, and to God the Judge of all, and to the spirits of just men made perfect, and to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel.’ The Lord led me through this blessed sentence over and over again, first to this word and then to that, and showed me wonderful glory in every one of them. These words have also often been a great refreshment to my spirit since that time. Blessed be God for having mercy on me.

fields.title: A Brief Account of the Author’s Call to the Work of the Ministry
fields.body_html:
265. Now that I am speaking of my experience, I will put in a word or two here about my preaching of the Word, and about God’s dealings with me in that too. About five or six years after I had been awakened, and helped to see both my need of Jesus Christ our Lord and His worth, and enabled to risk my soul on Him, some of the ablest among the saints with us, I mean the ablest in judgment and holiness of life, as they saw it, perceived that God had counted me worthy to understand something of His will in His holy and blessed Word, and had given me some ability to express what I saw to others for their building up. So they asked me, and very earnestly, whether I would be willing at times to undertake to speak a word of encouragement to them in one of the meetings.

266. Though at first this greatly dismayed and abashed my spirit, they kept asking and urging me, so I agreed to their request. Twice, at two separate gatherings, though in private and with much weakness and frailty, I used my gift among them. At this they not only seemed to be moved and comforted, but solemnly declared, as in the sight of the great God, that they were, and they gave thanks to the Father of mercies for the grace given to me.

267. After this, when some of them went out into the country to teach, they would sometimes want me to go with them. There, though I did not yet use my gift openly, and dared not, I did sometimes speak a word of counsel more privately to the good people in those places as I came among them. They received it as the others had, rejoicing at God’s mercy to me and declaring that their souls were built up by it.

268. So, to be brief, at last, at the continued request of the church, and after solemn prayer to the Lord with fasting, I was more particularly called out and appointed to preach the Word more regularly and publicly, not only to and among those who believed, but also to offer the gospel to those who had not yet received its faith. About that time I clearly found in my mind a secret prompting towards it, though, I bless God, not out of a desire for empty glory, for at that time I was most severely afflicted with the fiery darts of the devil about my eternal state.

269. Even so, I could not be content unless I was found using my gift. I was greatly spurred on to this, not only by the constant wishes of the godly, but also by Paul’s words to the Corinthians: ‘I beseech you, brethren (ye know the household of Stephanas, that it is the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints), that ye submit yourselves unto such, and to every one that helpeth with us, and laboureth’ (1 Cor. 16:15-16).

270. By this text I was made to see that the Holy Spirit never intended people who have gifts and abilities to bury them in the earth, but rather commanded and stirred them up to use their gift, and also commended those who were apt and ready to do so: ‘They have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints.’ In those days this Scripture ran constantly through my mind, encouraging and strengthening me in this work for God. I was also encouraged by several other Scriptures, and by examples of the godly described both in the Word and in other old histories (Acts 8:4; 18:24-25; 1 Pet. 4:10; Rom. 12:6; Foxe’s Acts and Monuments).

271. So, though in myself the most unworthy of all the saints, I set about the work, with great fear and trembling at the sight of my own weakness. According to my gift and the measure of my faith, I preached the blessed gospel that God had shown me in the holy Word of truth. When the country heard of it, people came in by the hundreds to hear the Word, and from all parts, though for many different reasons.

272. And I thank God that He gave me some measure of tenderness and pity for their souls. This also drove me to work with great diligence and earnestness to find a word that might, if God would bless it, take hold of the conscience and awaken it. In this the good Lord regarded the desire of His servant, for I had not been preaching long before some began to be touched by the Word and to be greatly troubled in their minds as they grasped the greatness of their sin and their need of Jesus Christ.

273. But at first I could not believe that God would speak to anyone’s heart through me, for I still counted myself unworthy. Yet those who were touched like this would love me and have a special regard for me. And though I refused to accept that they had been awakened through me, they would still admit it and declare it before God’s saints. They would also bless God for me, unworthy wretch that I am, and count me God’s instrument who had shown them the way of salvation.

274. So, seeing them so steady in both their words and their actions, and pressing so earnestly in their hearts after the knowledge of Jesus Christ, rejoicing that God had ever sent me where they were, I began to conclude that it might be true that God had owned such a foolish person as me in His work. Then this word of God came to my heart with much sweet refreshment: ‘The blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon me; and I caused the widow’s heart to sing for joy’ (Job 29:13).

275. So I rejoiced at this. Indeed, the tears of those whom God awakened through my preaching were both a comfort and an encouragement to me. For I thought of those sayings, ‘Who is he that maketh me glad but the same which is made sorry by me?’ (2 Cor. 2:2), and again, Though ‘I be not an apostle to others, yet doubtless I am to you: for the seal of mine apostleship are ye in the Lord’ (1 Cor. 9:2). So these things were another argument to me that God had called me to this work and stood by me in it.

276. In preaching the Word I took special notice of one thing: that the Lord led me to begin where His Word begins with sinners, that is, to condemn all flesh, and to open up and declare that the curse of God, through the law, belongs to and takes hold of everyone as they come into the world, because of sin. I carried out this part of my work with deep feeling, for the terrors of the law and guilt for my sins lay heavy on my conscience. I preached what I felt, what I felt painfully, the very thing under which my poor soul groaned and trembled to the point of astonishment.

277. Indeed, I have been like someone sent to them from the dead. I went in chains myself to preach to them in chains, and I carried in my own conscience the fire I urged them to beware of. I can truly say, without pretending, that when I have gone to preach I have gone full of guilt and terror right up to the pulpit door. There it has been lifted off me, and I have been free in my mind until I finished my work. Then immediately, even before I could get down the pulpit stairs, I have been as bad as I was before. Yet God carried me on, though surely with a strong hand, for neither guilt nor hell could take me off my work.

278. I went on like this for about two years, crying out against people’s sins and their fearful state because of them. After that the Lord came in on my own soul with some settled peace and comfort through Christ, for He gave me many sweet discoveries of His blessed grace through Him. So now my preaching changed, for I still preached what I saw and felt. So now I worked hard to hold out Jesus Christ to the world in all His offices, relationships and benefits. I also tried to uncover, condemn and remove the false supports and props on which the world leans, and by which it falls and perishes. I spent as long on these things as on the others.

279. After this, God led me into something of the mystery of union with Christ, so I opened that up and showed it to them as well. And when I had gone through these three main points of the Word of God, over about five years or more, I was caught in my present practice and thrown into prison. There I have now lain for more than as long again, to confirm the truth by suffering, as I had been testifying to it before by preaching, according to the Scriptures.

280. When I have been preaching, I thank God, my heart has often cried to God with great earnestness all through the service that He would make the Word effective for the salvation of the soul. I was always grieved for fear the enemy would take the Word away from the conscience, and so it would become unfruitful. So I worked hard to speak the Word in such a way that, if possible, the sin and the guilty person might be singled out by it.

281. Also, when I had finished the service, it went to my heart to think that the Word might now fall like rain on stony places. I kept wishing from my heart, Oh, if only those who heard me speak today could see as I do what sin, death, hell and the curse of God are, and also what the grace and love and mercy of God are, through Christ, to people in the state they are in, who are still estranged from Him! Indeed, I often said in my heart before the Lord that if being hanged at once before their eyes would be a means of awakening them and confirming them in the truth, I would gladly be content.

282. For in my preaching, especially when I have been occupied with the teaching of life by Christ without works, it has been as if an angel of God stood behind me to encourage me. Oh, it has come on my own soul with such power and heavenly evidence while I have been labouring to unfold it, prove it and fasten it on the consciences of others, that I could not be content with saying, I believe and am sure. It seemed to me that I was more than sure, if I may put it that way, that the things I was declaring were true.

283. When I first went out to preach the Word, the learned men and clergy of the area opened fire on me. But I was determined not to repay abuse with abuse, but to see how many of their worldly church members I could convince of their miserable state under the law, and of their need of Christ and His worth. For, I thought, this will answer for me in time to come, when they shall be for my hire before their faces (Gen. 30:33).

284. I never cared to meddle with matters that were controversial and disputed among the saints, especially matters of the least importance. Yet it pleased me greatly to contend with great earnestness for the word of faith and the forgiveness of sins through the death and sufferings of Jesus. But as for other things, I say, I would leave them alone, because I saw that they bred strife, and because neither doing them nor leaving them undone commended us to God as His. Besides, I saw that the work before me ran in another channel, namely to carry an awakening word. So I stuck to that and held to it.

285. I never tried to use other men’s work, and dared not (Rom. 15:18), though I do not condemn everyone who does. For I truly thought, and found by experience, that what was taught me by the Word and Spirit of Christ could be spoken, defended and stood by with the soundest and best-established conscience. And though I will not now say all I know on this matter, my experience has more of a share in this text of Scripture than many people realise (Gal. 1:11-12).

286. If any of those who were awakened through my ministry later fell back, as too many sometimes did, I can truly say that their loss has meant more to me than if one of my own children, born of my body, had been going to its grave. I truly think I can say without offending the Lord that nothing has touched me so closely as that, unless it was the fear of losing the salvation of my own soul. I have felt as if I had fine buildings and estates in the places where my children were born. My heart has been so wrapped up in the glory of this excellent work that I counted myself more blessed and honoured by God through it than if He had made me emperor of the Christian world, or lord of all the glory of the earth without it. Oh, these words: ‘He which converteth the sinner from the error of his way shall save a soul from death’ (Jas. 5:20). ‘The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise’ (Prov. 11:30). ‘They that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever’ (Dan. 12:3). ‘For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of rejoicing? Are not even ye in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming? For ye are our glory and joy’ (1 Thess. 2:19-20). These, I say, with many others like them, have been great refreshments to me.

287. I have noticed that where I have had a work to do for God, I have first had, as it were, God moving on my spirit to want to preach there. I have also noticed that particular souls have been laid strongly on my heart and I have been stirred up to long for their salvation, and that these very souls have afterwards been given as the fruits of my ministry. I have also noticed that a word dropped in passing has done more work in a sermon than everything else that was said. Sometimes too, when I thought I was doing no good, I did the most of all, and at other times, when I thought I would catch them, I have fished for nothing.

288. I have also noticed that where there has been a work to do on sinners, the devil has begun to roar in people’s hearts and through the mouths of his servants. Indeed, often when the wicked world has raged most, souls have been awakened by the Word. I could give particular examples, but I refrain.

289. My great desire in carrying out my ministry was to get into the darkest places of the country, among the people furthest from any profession of faith. This was not because I could not bear the light, for I was not afraid to show my gospel to anyone, but because I found that my spirit leaned most towards the work of awakening and converting, and the Word I carried also led most that way. ‘Yea, so have I strived to preach the gospel, not where Christ was named, lest I should build upon another man’s foundation’ (Rom. 15:20).

290. In my preaching I have really been in pain, and have, as it were, laboured in childbirth to bring forth children to God. Nor could I be satisfied unless some fruit appeared in my work. If I was fruitless, it did not matter who praised me. But if I was fruitful, I did not care who condemned me. I have thought of the words, ‘He that winneth souls is wise’ (Prov. 11:30), and again, ‘Lo, children are an heritage of the Lord; and the fruit of the womb is his reward. As arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are children of the youth. Happy is the man that hath filled his quiver full of them; they shall not be ashamed, but they shall speak with the enemies in the gate’ (Ps. 127:3-5).

291. It gave me no pleasure to see people drink in opinions if they seemed ignorant of Jesus Christ and of the worth of their own salvation. Sound conviction of sin, especially of unbelief, and a heart set on fire to be saved by Christ, with strong longing for a truly sanctified soul: that was what delighted me. Those were the souls I counted blessed.

292. But in this work, as in every other, I had my temptations, and of different kinds. Sometimes I would be attacked with great discouragement in it, fearing that I would not be able to speak the Word to people’s building up at all; indeed, that I would not be able to speak sense to the people. At such times such a strange faintness and weakness would seize my body that my legs could hardly carry me to the place of the service.

293. At other times, when I have been preaching, I have been violently attacked with blasphemous thoughts and strongly tempted to speak the words aloud before the congregation. At some times too, even when I began to speak the Word with great clearness, evidence and freedom of speech, before the end of that occasion I have been so blinded and so estranged from the things I was speaking about, and so tongue-tied before the people, that it was as if I did not know or remember what I was doing, or as if my head had been in a bag the whole time.

294. Again, sometimes when I have been about to preach on some sharp and scorching part of the Word, I have found the tempter suggesting, What, will you preach this? This condemns you. Your own soul is guilty of this. So do not preach on it at all; or if you do, water it down so as to leave yourself a way of escape, in case instead of awakening others you lay a guilt on your own soul that you will never get out from under.

295. But I thank the Lord that I have been kept from consenting to these horrible suggestions. Instead, like Samson, I have bowed myself with all my might to condemn sin and transgression wherever I found it, even though in doing so I brought guilt on my own conscience. ‘Let me die,’ I thought, ‘with the Philistines’ (Judg. 16:29-30), rather than deal dishonestly with the blessed Word of God. ‘Thou that teachest another, teachest not thou thyself?’ It is far better to judge yourself, even by preaching plainly to others, than to save yourself by imprisoning the truth in unrighteousness. Blessed be God for His help in this too.

296. While engaged in this blessed work of Christ, I have also often been tempted to pride and to having my heart lifted up. Though I dare not say I have not been infected with this, truly the Lord in His precious mercy has dealt with me in such a way that for the most part I have had little pleasure in giving way to such a thing. For it has been my daily portion to be let into the evil of my own heart, and to be made to see such a crowd of corruptions and weaknesses there that it has made me hang my head in spite of all my gifts and achievements. I have felt this thorn in the flesh to be the very mercy of God to me (2 Cor. 12:7-9).

297. Along with this I have also had some notable passage of the Word or other set before me, containing some sharp and piercing sentence about the soul perishing in spite of gifts and abilities. For example, this has been of great use to me: ‘Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, and a tinkling cymbal’ (1 Cor. 13:1-2).

298. A tinkling cymbal is a musical instrument on which a skilful player can make such melodious and heart-stirring music that everyone who hears him play can hardly keep from dancing. And yet, look, the cymbal has no life, and the music does not come from it, but from the skill of the one who plays it. So in the end the instrument may come to nothing and perish, even though such music was once made on it.

299. I saw that it is and will be just like this with those who have gifts but lack saving grace. They are in the hand of Christ as the cymbal was in the hand of David. And just as David could use the cymbal to make such joy in the service of God as to lift up the hearts of the worshippers, so Christ can use these gifted people to move the souls of His people in His church. Yet when He has done it all, He hangs them up as lifeless, though sounding, cymbals.

300. So this thought, together with some others, was for the most part like a hammer on the head of pride and the desire for empty glory. What, I thought, am I to be proud because I am sounding brass? Is it such a great thing to be a fiddle? Does not the smallest creature that has life have more of God in it than these? Besides, I knew it was love that would never die, but these must cease and vanish. So I concluded that a little grace, a little love, a little of the true fear of God is better than all these gifts. Indeed, I am fully convinced that it is possible for a soul who can hardly give anyone an answer without great confusion of method, I say it is possible for such a person to have a thousand times more grace, and so to be more in the love and favour of the Lord, than some who by virtue of the gift of knowledge can express themselves like angels.

301. So I came to see that although gifts in themselves were good for the purpose they are meant for, namely the building up of others, yet on their own they are empty and without power to save the soul of the one who has them. Nor, on their own, are they any sign that a person’s state is a happy one. They are only something God entrusts to some people, who must give an account of how they used or did not use them, when a little more life is over, to Him who is ready to judge the living and the dead.

302. This also showed me that gifts on their own were dangerous, not in themselves, but because of the evils that go with those who have them, namely pride, the desire for empty glory, conceit and so on. All of these were easily puffed up by the applause and praise of every thoughtless Christian, putting a poor creature in danger of falling into the condemnation of the devil.

303. So I saw that the one who has gifts needs to be let into a sight of their nature, namely that they fall short of putting him in a truly saved condition, in case he rests in them and so falls short of the grace of God.

304. He also has reason to walk humbly with God and be small in his own eyes, and to remember too that his gifts are not his own but the church’s, that by them he is made a servant to the church, and that in the end he must give an account of his stewardship to the Lord Jesus. And to give a good account will be a blessed thing.

305. So let everyone value a little with the fear of the Lord. Gifts are indeed desirable, but great grace and small gifts are better than great gifts and no grace. It does not say, the Lord gives gifts and glory, but the Lord gives grace and glory. And blessed is the one to whom the Lord gives grace, true grace, for that is a sure forerunner of glory.

306. But when Satan saw that his tempting and attacking me like this would not serve his purpose, namely to overthrow my ministry and make it fail in its aims, he tried another way. This was to stir up the minds of the ignorant and malicious to load me with slanders and insults. So now I can say that whatever the devil could devise and his agents invent was whirled up and down the country against me, thinking, as I said, that by this means they would make me abandon my ministry.

307. So it began to be rumoured up and down among the people that I was a witch, a Jesuit, a highwayman and the like.

308. To all of this I will only say that God knows I am innocent. But as for my accusers, let them prepare to meet me before the judgment seat of the Son of God, to answer there for these things along with all the rest of their sins, unless God gives them repentance for them, which I pray for with all my heart.

309. But what was reported with the boldest confidence was that I had my mistresses, my whores, my illegitimate children, even two wives at once, and the like. Now I glory in these slanders along with the others, because they are only slanders, foolish or wicked lies and falsehoods thrown at me by the devil and his offspring. And if I were not treated so wickedly by the world, I would lack one mark of a saint and a child of God. ‘Blessed are ye (said the Lord Jesus) when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely for my sake; rejoice, and be exceeding glad, for great is your reward in heaven; for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you’ (Matt. 5:11).

310. So on my own account these things do not trouble me, no, not even if they were twenty times more than they are. I have a good conscience, and whereas they speak evil of me as an evildoer, those who falsely accuse my good conduct in Christ will be ashamed.

311. So then, what shall I say to those who have smeared me like this? Shall I threaten them? Shall I scold them? Shall I flatter them? Shall I beg them to hold their tongues? No, not I. If it were not that these things make those who start and spread them ripe for damnation, I would say to them, Report it, because it will increase my glory.

312. So I bind these lies and slanders to me as an ornament. It belongs to my Christian profession to be vilified, slandered, insulted and reviled. And since all this is nothing else, as my God and my conscience bear me witness, I rejoice in insults for Christ’s sake.

313. I also call all those fools or rogues who have made it any part of their business to claim any of the things mentioned above about me, namely that I have been immoral with other women or the like, to do this: when they have tried their very hardest and made the fullest inquiry they can, let them truly prove against me that there is any woman in heaven, or on earth, or in hell, who can say that I have at any time, in any place, by day or night, so much as tried to be immoral with her. And am I saying this to beg my enemies to think well of me? No, not I. I will beg no one for relief in this. Believe me or disbelieve me in this; it is all the same to me.

314. My enemies have missed their target in shooting at me like this. I am not the man. I wish they themselves were as innocent. If all the fornicators and adulterers in England were hanged by the neck until they were dead, John Bunyan, the object of their envy, would still be alive and well. Apart from my wife, I do not know whether there is such a thing as a woman breathing under the whole canopy of heaven, except by their clothes, their children or common report.

315. And in this I admire the wisdom of God, that He made me shy of women from my first conversion until now. Those I have been most closely involved with know, and can bear me witness, that it is a rare thing to see me act in a familiar way towards a woman. I loathe the common greeting of a woman with a kiss; it is odious to me in whoever I see it. I cannot stand being alone in their company. I seldom so much as touch a woman’s hand, for I think these things are not fitting for me. When I have seen good men greet with a kiss the women they have visited, or who have visited them, I have at times objected to it. And when they have answered that it was only a matter of politeness, I have told them that it is not a seemly sight. Some indeed have pointed to the holy kiss. But then I have asked why they made exceptions, why they greeted the most attractive and let the plain ones go. So however praiseworthy such things have been in the eyes of others, they have been unseemly in my sight.

316. And now, to wind up this matter, I call not only on men but on angels to prove me guilty of having sexual relations with any woman except my wife. Nor am I afraid to do it a second time, knowing that I cannot offend the Lord in such a case, to call on God as witness on my soul that I am innocent in these things. Not that I have been kept like this because of any goodness in me more than in anyone else; but God has been merciful to me and has kept me. I pray to Him that He will keep me still, not only from this but from every evil way and work, and preserve me for His heavenly kingdom. Amen.

317. Now just as Satan worked through insults and slanders to make me vile among my countrymen, so that if possible my preaching might come to nothing, a long and wearisome imprisonment was added to this, so that I might be frightened away from my service for Christ, and the world terrified and made afraid to hear me preach. I will now give you a brief account of this.

fields.title: A Brief Account of the Author’s Imprisonment
fields.body_html:
318. I had professed the glorious gospel of Christ for a long time, and had preached it for about five years, when I was arrested at a meeting of good people in the country. Had they left me alone, I would have preached to them that day. But they took me away from among them and brought me before a magistrate. Although I offered a guarantee that I would appear at the next sessions, he still committed me to prison, because those who stood surety for me would not agree to be bound that I would preach to the people no more.

319. At the sessions I was charged with being an upholder and supporter of unlawful assemblies and illegal religious meetings, and with not conforming to the national worship of the Church of England. After some discussion there with the magistrates, they took my plain dealing with them as a confession, as they called it, of the charge, and sentenced me to permanent banishment because I refused to conform. So, being handed over again to a jailer, I was taken back to prison, and I have now lain there a full twelve years, waiting to see what God would allow those men to do with me.

320. In this condition I have remained with much contentment, through grace. But I have met with many ups and downs in my heart, from the Lord, from Satan and from my own corruption. Through all of them, glory be to Jesus Christ, I have also received, among many things, much conviction, instruction and understanding. I will not discuss these at length here, but only give you a hint or two, a word that may stir up the godly to bless God and to pray for me, and also to take courage, should the case ever be their own, not to fear what man can do to them.

321. Never in all my life have I had such a great entrance into the Word of God as now. Scriptures I saw nothing in before were made to shine on me in this place and state. Jesus Christ also was never more real and evident than now. Here I have truly seen and felt Him. Oh, that word, We have not preached unto you cunningly devised fables (2 Pet. 1:16), and that one, God raised Christ from the dead, and gave him glory, that your faith and hope might be in God, were blessed words to me in this imprisoned condition of mine.

322. These three or four Scriptures have also been great refreshments to me in this condition: John 14:1-4; John 16:33; Col. 3:3-4; Heb. 12:22-24. So sometimes, when I have been tasting their sweetness, I have been able to laugh at destruction and to fear neither the horse nor its rider. In this place I have had sweet sights of the forgiveness of my sins and of my being with Jesus in another world. Oh, Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, the countless company of angels, and God the judge of all, and the spirits of just men made perfect, and Jesus (Heb. 12:22-24), have been sweet to me in this place. I have seen things here that I am persuaded I will never be able to express while I am in this world. I have seen the truth of this Scripture: “Whom having not seen, ye love; in whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory” (1 Pet. 1:8).

323. I never knew what it was for God to stand by me at every turn, and at every attempt of Satan to afflict me and so on, as I have found Him since I came in here. For just as fears have presented themselves, so have supports and encouragements. Indeed, when I have been startled, as it were, by nothing but my own shadow, God, being very tender towards me, has not let me be troubled, but would strengthen me against everything with one Scripture or another. So much so that I have often said, If it were right to do so, I could pray for greater trouble for the sake of greater comfort (Eccles. 7:14; 2 Cor. 1:5).

324. Before I came to prison I saw what was coming, and two considerations especially lay warm on my heart. The first was how I would be able to endure if my imprisonment should be long and wearisome. The second was how I would be able to face death, if that should be my lot. For the first of these, this Scripture was a great instruction to me (Col. 1:11): to pray to God “to be strengthened with all might, according to his glorious power, unto all patience and long-suffering with joyfulness.” For no less than a whole year before I was imprisoned, I could hardly go to prayer without this sentence or sweet petition pushing itself, as it were, into my mind and persuading me that if I was ever to go through long suffering, I must have patience, especially if I was to endure it joyfully.

325. As for the second consideration, this saying was of great use to me: “But we had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead” (2 Cor. 1:9). By this Scripture I was made to see that if I was ever to suffer rightly, I must first pass a sentence of death on everything that can properly be called a thing of this life, even reckoning myself, my wife, my children, my health, my pleasures and everything as dead to me, and myself as dead to them.

326. The second thing was to live on God who is invisible, as Paul said in another place. The way not to lose heart is to “Look not on the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2 Cor. 4:18). And so I reasoned with myself: If I prepare only for a prison, then the whip catches me unawares, and so does the pillory. Again, if I prepare only for these, then I am not ready for banishment. And further, if I conclude that banishment is the worst, then if death comes I am taken by surprise. So I see that the best way to go through sufferings is to trust in God through Christ as regards the world to come, and as regards this world, to count the grave my house, to make my bed in darkness, to say to corruption, You are my father, and to the worm, You are my mother and sister; that is, to make myself familiar with these things.

327. But in spite of these helps, I found myself a man surrounded by weaknesses. Parting from my wife and poor children has often been to me in this place like having the flesh torn from my bones. This was not only because I am rather too fond of these great mercies, but also because I would often call to mind the many hardships, miseries and needs that my poor family was likely to meet with if I were taken from them, especially my poor blind child, who lay nearer my heart than all the rest. Oh, the thought of the hardship I imagined my poor blind one might go through would break my heart to pieces.

328. Poor child, I thought, what sorrow you are likely to have as your lot in this world! You will be beaten, will have to beg, will suffer hunger, cold, nakedness and a thousand disasters, though now I cannot bear even the wind to blow on you. But then, pulling myself together, I thought, I must risk you all with God, though it cuts me to the quick to leave you. Oh, I saw that in this condition I was like a man pulling his house down on the heads of his wife and children. Yet I thought, I must do it, I must do it. And now I thought of those two milk cows that were to carry the ark of God into another country and leave their calves behind them (1 Sam. 6:10).

329. But what helped me in this temptation was several considerations, of which I will name three in particular here. The first was the thought of these two Scriptures: “Leave thy fatherless children, I will preserve them alive, and let thy widows trust in me.” And again, “The Lord said, Verily it shall be well with thy remnant, verily I will cause the enemy to entreat thee well in the time of evil” (Jer. 49:11; 15:11).

330. I also had this consideration: that if I risked everything for God, I bound God to take care of my concerns. But if I forsook Him in His ways for fear of any trouble that might come to me or mine, then I would not only prove my profession false, but would also be reckoning that my concerns were not as safe left at God’s feet, while I stood up for His name, as they would be in my own care, even at the cost of denying the way of God. This was a stinging thought, and like spurs in my flesh. That Scripture also helped greatly to fasten it on me, where Christ prays against Judas that God would frustrate him in the selfish thoughts that moved him to sell his master. Please read it soberly: Psalm 109:6-20.

331. I also had another consideration, and that was the dread of the torments of hell, which I was sure must be the lot of those who, for fear of the cross, shrink back from their profession of Christ, His words and His laws before others. I also thought of the glory He had prepared for those who, in faith and love and patience, stood by His ways before others. These things, I say, have helped me when thoughts of the misery that both I and my family might be exposed to for the sake of my profession have lain pinching on my mind.

332. When I have imagined that I might be banished for my profession, I have thought of this Scripture: “They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented; (of whom the world was not worthy)” (Heb. 11:37-38), even though the people thought them too bad to live and stay among them. I have also thought of this saying: “The Holy Ghost witnesseth in every city,” “that bonds and afflictions abide me” (Acts 20:23). I truly think that my soul and that saying have sometimes reasoned together about the sore and sad state of banishment and exile, how those in it were exposed to hunger, cold, dangers, nakedness, enemies and a thousand disasters, and at last, perhaps, to die in a ditch like a poor, abandoned sheep. But I thank God that so far I have not been moved by these most tender reasonings, but rather by them have shown my heart all the more true to God.

333. I will tell you a curious story. Once, more than at any other time, I was in a very sad and low condition for many weeks. At that time, being only a new prisoner and not familiar with the laws, I had this weighing heavily on my spirit: that for all I could tell, my imprisonment might end at the gallows. So Satan pressed hard on me to make me lose heart, suggesting this to me: But what if, when you actually come to die, you are in this condition, that is, unable to taste the things of God, and without any evidence on your soul of a better state hereafter? For indeed at this time all the things of God were hidden from my soul.

334. So when I first began to think about this, it troubled me greatly. For I thought to myself that in the condition I was then in I was not fit to die, nor did I think I could die well if I were called to. Besides, I thought to myself that even if I managed somehow to scramble up the ladder, I would still, by shaking or other signs of fainting, give the enemy occasion to scorn the way of God and His people for their timidity. So this weighed on me with great trouble, for it seemed to me that I would be ashamed to die with a pale face and shaking knees in such a cause as this.

335. So I prayed to God that He would comfort me and give me strength to do and suffer whatever He should call me to. Yet no comfort appeared, but everything remained hidden. At this time too I was so truly taken up with the thought of death that it was often as if I were on the ladder with a rope around my neck. Only this was some encouragement to me: I thought I might now have an opportunity to speak my last words to a crowd, which I thought would come to see me die. And I thought, if it must be so, if God will convert even one soul through my last words, I will not count my life thrown away or lost.

336. But still all the things of God were kept out of my sight, and the tempter kept following me with, But where must you go when you die? What will become of you? Where will you be found in another world? What evidence do you have for heaven and glory, and an inheritance among those who are sanctified? So I was tossed about for many weeks and did not know what to do. At last this thought fell on me with weight: that it was for the word and way of God that I was in this condition. So I was bound not to flinch a hair’s breadth from it.

337. I also thought that God might choose whether He would give me comfort now or at the hour of death, but that did not mean I might choose whether to hold to my profession or not. I was bound, but He was free. Indeed, it was my duty to stand by His word, whether He would ever look on me or save me in the end. So, I thought, the matter being like this, I am for going on and risking my eternal state with Christ, whether I have comfort here or not. If God does not come in, I thought, I will leap off the ladder even blindfold into eternity, sink or swim, come heaven, come hell. Lord Jesus, if You will catch me, do; if not, I will take the risk for Your name.

338. No sooner was I settled in this resolution than this word dropped on me: Doth Job serve God for nought? It was as if the accuser had said, Lord, Job is not an upright man; he serves You for ulterior motives. Have You not put a hedge around him? But stretch out Your hand now and touch all that he has, and he will curse You to Your face. Well now, I thought, is this the sign of an upright soul, to want to serve God when everything is taken from him? Is he a godly man who will serve God for nothing rather than give up? Blessed be God; then I hope I have an upright heart, for I am resolved, God giving me strength, never to deny my profession, though I should have nothing at all for my pains. And as I was thinking about this, this Scripture was set before me: Psalm 44:12-26.

339. Now my heart was full of comfort, for I hoped it was sincere. I would not have been without this trial for a great deal. I am comforted every time I think of it, and I hope I will bless God for ever for what it has taught me. I could tell of many more of God’s dealings with me, but these, out of the spoils won in battles, I have dedicated to maintain the house of God (1 Chron. 26:27).

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
THE CONCLUSION

1. Of all the temptations I have ever met with in my life, the temptation to question the existence of God and the truth of His gospel is the worst, and the hardest to bear. When this temptation comes, it takes my belt away from me and removes the foundations from under me. Oh, I have often thought of the words, ‘Have your loins girt about with truth’, and of these, ‘When the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?’

2. Sometimes, after committing sin, when I have expected severe discipline from the hand of God, the very next thing I have had from Him has been a discovery of His grace. Sometimes, when I have been comforted, I have called myself a fool for sinking so low under trouble. And then again, when I have been cast down, I thought I was unwise to give way to comfort like that. Both of these have weighed on me with such strength and weight.

3. I have wondered greatly at this one thing: that although God visits my soul with ever so blessed a discovery of Himself, I have found that afterwards hours have come on me when my spirit has been so filled with darkness that I could not even once imagine what that God and that comfort were by which I had been refreshed.

4. I have sometimes seen more in one line of the Bible than I could well bear to stand under, and yet at another time the whole Bible has been as dry as a stick to me. Or rather, my heart has been so dead and dry towards it that I could not draw the smallest drop of refreshment from it, though I have looked it all over.

5. Of all tears, the best are those produced by the blood of Christ; and of all joy, the sweetest is that which is mixed with mourning over Christ. Oh, it is a fine thing to be on our knees before God with Christ in our arms. I hope I know something of these things.

6. To this day I find seven abominations in my heart: (1) Leanings towards unbelief. (2) Suddenly forgetting the love and mercy that Christ shows. (3) A leaning towards the works of the law. (4) Wanderings and coldness in prayer. (5) Forgetting to watch for what I pray for. (6) A tendency to grumble because I have no more, and yet a readiness to misuse what I have. (7) I can do none of the things God commands me without my corruptions pushing themselves in: ‘When I would do good, evil is present with me.’

7. I constantly see and feel these things, and am afflicted and weighed down by them. Yet the wisdom of God orders them for my good. (1) They make me loathe myself. (2) They keep me from trusting my heart. (3) They convince me that all righteousness of my own is not enough. (4) They show me that I must flee to Jesus. (5) They press me to pray to God. (6) They show me my need to watch and be sober. (7) And they stir me to look to God through Christ to help me and carry me through this world. Amen.
